answer: `set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true` arms threshold-crossing supervision on the port; data-supervision true/false arms the collection itself. `add`/`set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> low-threshold <v> high-threshold <v>` sets the limit on that instance, with parameter = errored-seconds. `pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>` holds the per-type value and exposes default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value, e.g. `set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200`. pm-profile-entry carries default-tca-supervision for newly created resources. direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location all, na, near-end or far-end (default all).

`add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <sha-1|aes-cmac|sha-256|md5> key-value <value> [is-trusted true]` - key-id range 1..65534, key-value length 8..40, is-trusted default false. `add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <n>` - IPv4, IPv6 or DNS name; origin manual (default) or dhcp; auth-key-id default not-applicable; admin-state default unlock. `set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true` - ntp-enabled defaults true, ntp-auth-enabled false, assignment-method manual, dhcp or both (default both). Verify with `show ntp-server-status-<ip>`: auth-status ok, yes, bad or none (default none), and reach, an 8-bit shift register where 377 means all recent probes were answered, plus stratum, offset, jitter and condition (sys.peer). `show ntp ntp-active-server` names the server in use and `show clock time-source` should read ntp.

`protection-switch` moves traffic, `manual-switchover` moves the controller. `protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<force|lockout|manual|release> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>`, Operational mode; switch-target is not needed for the release and lockout operations. Example: `protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection`. The persistent equivalent is protection-group pg-request (clear default, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout, exercise). `manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<AID>` takes a card AID, e.g. `manual-switchover card-1-3`, and prompts: Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost.

`set-time` is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, which is what rejects it. `show clock` gives time-source (ntp or manual, default manual), current-time, universal-time, timezone, DST-active and last-time-jump (jumps of less than 10 seconds are ignored). If it reads ntp, check `show ntp ntp-enabled` and `show ntp-server-status-<ip>` for reach (377 = all probes answered), offset and condition. To set it by hand, `set ntp ntp-enabled false`, then `set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z` - ISO 8601 combined date and time, Z for UTC or +/-hh:mm for another zone. `time` prints the current time using the system-configured timezone, not the one given to set-time. Timezone is `set clock timezone <value>`, default Universal-Time-Coordinated.

`show ne` identifies the node: ne-id, ne-name (default '1830 GX'), ne-type (G30 or G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), ne-site, ne-location, clli, node-controller-chassis-name (default 1), recover-mode. `status`, or `status system`, is the dashboard: name/id/type, active and inactive SW labels, uptime, management IP, alarm counts per severity and an equipment summary; `status equipment [chassis-id]` trees chassis, cards and toms. `show slot` gives supported-type versus installed-type per position. The cost: `restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]`. With no resource-id the active controller card restarts; with no type a warm restart is done. cold reboots all components and is service affecting, connectivity back within five minutes; warm reboots the processor and is non service affecting; shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. Confirmation is required unless -f.

The occupant is `card-1-2` (card-<name>, keyed by chassis-name and slot-name). Beneath a card hang comm-eth, inventory, port, property, sub-component, tom and usb; beneath each port hang current-fw, serdes and supported-tom-power. The holder `slot-1-2` also carries current-fw and reports supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment. The pluggable is `tom-<card-name>-<port-name>`, e.g. tom-1-2-T1, with required-type CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS. Its FRU inventory is read with `show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>`, e.g. `show inventory-1-3-1`: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class (1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status.

Model capability comes from the show-only supported-* family. `show supported-card-<card-type>` gives node-type-compatibility (all, ILA, OADM), supported-subtype, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. Per port, `show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>` gives port-type, direction, configuration-mode, faceplate-label, default-tom and allows-auto-migration; also supported-slot, supported-chassis, supported-tom and tom-type. What the installed unit is doing is `show card-<name>`: required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, category, chassis-name, slot-name, power-profile, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state.

Instance, then area, then interface, then the neighbor appears. `add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad>` - instance-id 0..255, version ospfv2 (default) or ospfv3, router-id-mode manual or use-loopback (default use-loopback); with use-loopback an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. `add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>` - the OSPF instance must be created before the area. `add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>` - instance and area must be present; ospf-if-name is a leafref to an existing interface if-name; enable default true, hello-interval default 10 (1..32767 s), router-dead-interval default 40 (4..65535 s), ospf-cost default 10, priority default 1. `show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<area-id>/<if-name>/<router-id>` shows how far it got: state down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading or full, and role drother, dr, bdr or ptp. Both NEs must have instance, area and interface and be connected with DCN interface bridges; the neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

`show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>` is the per-card view, e.g. `show software-load-1-5/active`; swload-state is active, inactive or installable. It reports swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status (validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete, failed or timeout), swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-pkg-type. The pieces are `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>` with state installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown, plus version and description, and one level deeper `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`. The bundled firmware is `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> fw-version`, and versions of the same firmware differ per equipment-type.

`show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress` answers it: total-frames-out is what you transmit, total-frames-in what you receive, and error-frames, total-discarded-frames, total-discarded-tlvs, total-unrecognized-tlvs and total-ageouts show what is being thrown away; all default 0, bounded by last-change-time and last-clear-time. Counters for a port freeze whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled on that port, and the egress direction is not supported. `show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress` shows what was learned (chassis-id, port-id, system-name, ttl, age, last-update) and is kept indefinitely until the port is decommissioned or cleared. `show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port>` shows what you advertise: chassis-id is the chassis serial number, port-id the port AID, system-name the NE name. `show lldp hold-on-timer` defaults to 900 seconds and applies when a neighbor sends no TTL TLV.

`show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>`, or `show slot` for all positions, gives AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment, so an empty installed-type against a populated supported-type is a vacant slot. FRU detail for the occupant is `show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>`: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date and fw-status (not-applicable, current, not-current or unavailable). Firmware level is `show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>`, also addressable as current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name>, returning fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status current, not-current or unavailable (default unavailable). `show equipment` and `status equipment` give the rolled-up view.

`show manifest-<manifest-file>` gives manifest-signature, downloaded-on and information. The contents split two ways: `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, where state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), and `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` for the firmware carried in it. `show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>` displays the packaged FRU information for one equipment-type, and `show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature]` covers the image files. For progress rather than per-package state, `show upgrade-status-<resource>` reports at ne, chassis or card level with to-swload-version, status, start-time, end-time, step and details.

Alarm severity defaults sit in alarm-severity-profile, whose rows are alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location>, e.g. `set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor`. Severities are critical, event, major, minor, not-reported and warning; direction na, ingress or egress; location na, near-end or far-end; show also exposes service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). Both objects are system-managed and cannot be manually deleted. PM defaults come from pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>, whose default-data-supervision and default-tca-supervision decide, for newly created resources of that type, whether data supervision and threshold-crossing supervision start enabled. Default limits per type are in pm-threshold-profile (default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value, max-value), and pm-profile global-data-supervision is auto-enabled or manual (default manual).

The decision is ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>. Its action is protect, bypass or discard (default protect), and priority (uint8, mandatory on add) gives precedence between SPD entries. Other attributes: ipsec-protocol ESP, mode tunnel (default) or transport, esn default true, anti-replay-window 32..1024 default 64 when action is protect, dynamic-ts default disabled. Beneath it hang ipsec-sa-proposal and ipsec-traffic-selector (next-layer-protocol any = 0, opaque = 255, or a number 0-255, default any); beneath the traffic selector hang local-subnet and remote-subnet, keyed by prefix, and local-ports and remote-ports, keyed by start and stop. The SPD entry sits under ikev2-peer, which sits under ikev2-local-instance. Example: `add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect`.

trusted-certificate is the CA you trust: the X509v3 root and intermediate certificates trusted by the system, and what every other certificate's trust-chain points at. local-certificate is this node's own X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing one of the secure application identities; it uniquely carries used-by, self-signed and subject-alternative-names. peer-certificate is the far end: the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application, with the extra white-listed attribute meaning it was imported without a trust chain. certificate is not a holder at all but the action command - `show certificates`, `show certificate-revocation`, `clear certificate type=<trusted|local|peer> id=<id>`. All three share version v3, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, valid-from, valid-to, status, public-key-length (rsa2048/3072/4096, ecdsa256/384/521) and revocation-mode auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked (default auto).

Import with `import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]`, Operational mode, PEM format. The type is local-certificate, peer-certificate or trusted-certificate, e.g. `import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=trusted-cert-1 <string in PEM format>`. -i also imports the intermediate certificates in a bundle, or those named by the AIA extension of a single-certificate file; root certificates must be installed individually. Without a certificate-name the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix. passphrase applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. Material can also be created locally with cert-gen (self-signed, days default 365, auto-install default true) or csr-gen, which leaves a local-certificate in pending-import state. Removal is `clear [-f] certificate [type=]<trusted|local|peer> [id=]<id>`; the id must match a currently installed but unused certificate, and purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused are accepted in place of a type.

access-rule permits or denies: `add access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name> action <permit|deny>`, with action mandatory on add and filters path (default *), module-name (default *), attribute, attribute-value and operation (create, read, update, delete, execute; default *). access-rule-list fixes the evaluation order: it groups access-rules by user-group and is processed in order as given by sequence-id, lower ids first. sw-control-rule has nothing to do with traffic - it overrides the default action on software service failure, with fail-action default-action, ignore or system-restart. IP packet filtering itself is acl (type IPv4 or IPv6, interface 1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-B, DCN-2, DCN-2-B) and its ace entries, whose action is drop (default), accept or reject.

Order is set by sequence-id: the access-rule-list is processed in order as given by sequence-id, and within it lower number ids are processed first, so the lower sequence-id wins. sequence-id is a uint16 on both access-rule and access-rule-list and can be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries; if not provided it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, so the rule goes to the end of the list. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists. The access-rule-list user-group attribute is a leaf-list of user-group names whose default '*' matches all existing user-groups, and a maximum of 20 user-groups can be referenced. Example: `add access-rule-list-A user-group XY`.

It is not in snmp-community: the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Set it there with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [trap-community-string <value>]` or `set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>`. trap-community-string is a string of length 0..32 and defaults to infinera, which is what a receiver expecting something else rejects. Other snmp-target attributes: enabled default true, snmp-version v2c (default) or v3, snmpv3-user only when snmp-version is v3, target-port default 162 (range 0..65535), target-transport udp. snmp-community-<name>, with community-string of length 1..32 and community-string-access read-only, governs polling access rather than traps. Globally, `set snmp enabled true port 161`.

external-fiber-connection is the one written for you: it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it can be configured manually that is not recommended. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations. Attributes: src-node-id, src-card-name, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-card-name, dst-port-name, label, fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way (default two-way), and scope general-purpose or cable-id (default general-purpose) - if scope is not cable-id, CableID verification excludes that connection from the CableID path. By contrast fiber-connection is user-provisioned and links two distinct ports or sub-ports within the same NE, and supporting-fiber-connection is show-only, listing the fiber-connection-list path.

Use ipv4-address: `add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>`, for example `add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0`; show adds origin static (default), dhcp or auto-config. Addresses beginning with 0, with 127, or in 224 through 255 are disallowed and only valid netmasks are accepted, and a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. The two look-alikes are read-only LLDP data, not configuration: management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports the management addresses advertised by a remote system as received on a local port, and management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports those this node advertises. Both only expose if-subtype (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), if-id and address-oid.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface, which is the usual refusal. Check `show interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method` - static (default) or dhcp - and ipv4-enabled (default true), and switch it with `set interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method static`. The address must also be legal: addresses beginning with 0, with 127, or in 224 through 255 are disallowed, and only valid netmasks may be configured. To see which interfaces exist, press ? after `ipv4-address-` for the object completion options, or run `show interface`, which lists if-type (ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp, hdlc), supporting-port, admin-state and oper-state. `show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> origin` reveals whether an existing address is static, dhcp or auto-config.

Everything in use is under route: `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>` lists system routes from all sources and reports source-protocol (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) plus special-next-hop none (default), blackhole or unreachable. Routes live in RIBs - `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]`, address-family ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast, one system-controlled default RIB per address family per routing instance - and resolved hops are `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface>`, e.g. `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`. Hand-typed routes are added with `add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <v>] [advertised <true|false>] [distance <1..255>] [interface <v>] [origin <manual|dhcp>] [special-next-hop blackhole]`; advertised defaults false, distance 1, origin manual. ipv6-static-route is the IPv6 equivalent.

local-ports and remote-ports belong to the security tunnel. Both are keyed <ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop> and nest under ipsec-traffic-selector, supporting only add, show and delete. start takes all, opaque or a port number; stop is a port number defaulting to 0, and 0 is accepted only when start is all or opaque. Examples: `add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53`, `add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all`. connection-ports is the connectivity one: `show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]`, show-only, nested under a degree. degree-number is 1..20 and must not exceed max-degrees; index has range 1..2 but is always 1 in the 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bidirectional; port-name is the dwdm-line port of an RD or ILAx card.

`take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]` makes the copy, Operational mode. db-instance is temp (default, temporary storage for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent), or the automatic onehour, oneday, oneweek, plus rollback; type is db-backup (default) or system-backup; description up to 128 characters. Re-taking an existing instance overwrites it. It is refused unless the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption is configured, either globally in security-policies or as a parameter here: minimum 40 characters, no dictionary words, characters from the 85-character Z85 set. `activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]` puts it back, sanity-check-override default false, pre-condition being that a snapshot must have been taken. `show database-<database-type>` (active, manual, oneday, onehour, oneweek, rollback, temp) lists them with backup-time and description.

activate (Operational mode) is one verb over many targets: activate swimage activates the currently installable image and implies a system restart (db-action auto|empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback, default auto; optional label; -f skips the confirmation prompt). activate database activates the currently inactive database, also implying a restart (db-instance active|manual|oneday|onehour|oneweek|rollback|temp, db-passphrase string 40..200, restart-type cold|warm default cold, sanity-check-override true|false default false). activate location-led starts an LED location or lamp test on a chassis or card (led-mode flash|solid, default flash; timeout 0..120 s, default 0 meaning no timeout; only one test at a time). activate eqpt-fw activates a firmware image on a chassis/card/tom (resource plus fw-image-name). activate krp installs a Key Replacement Package. activate otdr and activate otdr-fiber-check trigger OTDR measurements, activate loopback enables WSS loopback on an NMC, and activate activate-file activates a file. For the database case there is also a separate command: activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>], which activates an available database snapshot. Its pre-condition is that a snapshot must have been taken (see take-snapshot); db-instance defaults to temp, paraphrase is a string of length 40..200, and sanity-check-override defaults to false.

capabilities is the per-card one: show capabilities-<name>, where name is the card name (string); it retrieves the capability information of a card. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. l0-capabilities is the photonic one: show l0-capabilities takes no parameters at all and shows the capability details related to the node's Layer 0 functions. oadm-capabilities is the add/drop one: show oadm-capabilities [max-degrees] [max-adgs] reports the maximum number of degrees (uint8, value 20; 0 if not supported, and degrees are only supported on OADM node types, ILA being 0 by convention because it has exactly 2 fixed directions) and the maximum number of Add/Drop Groups (uint8, value 110; 0 if not supported, ADGs also only on OADM node types). The note in the guide is that max-degrees is the maximum working degree-number, not necessarily the supported deployment configuration. All three are show-only and run in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

show controller-card-<name> displays just the controller card, with redundancy-status (active, standby, not-in-service; default not-in-service), redundancy-standby-status (ready-synchronized, not-ready-synchronizing, not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out, card-not-present; default not-ready-synchronizing), number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover (both only visible on the active controller), and additional-details (string 0..128). card is the generic card-base object with attributes common to every card type: add/set/show/delete card-<name>, with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name (settable only at creation), power-profile, category, admin-state (lock/maintenance/unlock, default unlock), oper-state, avail-state, alarm-report-control (default inhibited), alias-name, label, parent-card, subcard-list, last-reboot-reason and last-reboot-time. For what a model of card supports, use show supported-card-<card-type>, which reports node-type-compatibility (all/ILA/OADM), supported-subtype, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. All three are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

macsec-entity is the Ethernet MACsec object: add/set/show/delete macsec-entity-<name> with supporting-facility (an ethernet facility), enabled (true/false, default true), link-security-control (must-secure or should-secure, default must-secure), replay-protection (enable/disable), replay-protection-window (0..4294967295, default 0), alarm-report-control (default inhibited) and label. Its cipher term is read-only: negotiated-cipher-suite on show; the configurable cipher choice lives in mka-policy (macsec-cipher-suite, plus key-server-priority, confidentiality-offset and sak-rekey-interval). secure-entity is the optical-line/L1 encryption object: add/set/show/delete secure-entity-<name> with supporting-facility and remote-secure-entity (the remote optical carrier on 1830 GX G40, the remote ODU on G30, or the remote OTUFlex for CHM7/CHM7x L1 service encryption), enabled (default false), re-key-frequency (3600..86400 seconds, default 28800), re-key-fail-policy (kill-traffic or continue-traffic, default continue-traffic) and traffic-kill-offset (0..86400 s, default 0, used only when the policy is kill-traffic). Its cipher terms are read via show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number>: encryption-algorithm aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length key-length-256, integrity-algorithm none, dh-group ecp-521.

ase-idler-service is the ASE idler filling function on a card: add/delete/set/show ase-idler-service-<name>, with ase-idler-enable (enabled/disabled, default disabled) to switch ASE idler filling of the unused and nmc-failed portions of the band spectrum, and the read-only ase-idler-state (ase-enabled, ase-partially-enabled, ase-faulted, ase-disabled; default ase-disabled) reporting whether filling is complete, incomplete or faulted. Its function is idler, and in SLTE that means the ASE idler functionality handled at the RD WSS even though the signal comes from elsewhere. ase-idler-source is the pump that produces the signal: set/show only, with pump-enable (enabled/disabled, default disabled), the read-only pump-state, target-output-power (-3.00..20.50 dBm, default 13), admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), and supporting-input-port and supporting-output-port. Its function value is ase-idler-source. sw-service does not belong with them: it is a software command, show sw-service-<sv-name> / show sw-services, listing OS services and containers with equipment, location, state (off/ok/fail), state-details, cpu-usage, memory-usage, uptime, last-start-time and reboot-count.

No, they are not harmless. change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<enabled|disabled> toggles Zero Touch Provisioning: change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot. change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and stops it if it is already running; the command can be run while ZTP is in progress, interrupting it. Use -f to skip the confirmation, and show ztp to read the current mode. clear [-f] recover-mode clears the recover-mode flag, which confirms the current configuration as is, re-enables communication with the line cards and potentially reconfigures the traffic settings, so the guide states it may be traffic impacting. It takes no parameters. By contrast the carrier-mode commands are read-only: show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode> and show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> only display carrier-mode information (capacity, client-mode ethernet or ethernet-otn, baud-rate, application, compatibility-id, status, supported-subtypes). Both change-ztp-mode and clear recover-mode are Operational mode only.

third-party-app shows and sets the application itself: set/show third-party-app-<app-name> with version, vendor, product, label, state (running, stopped, failed; default stopped), information (string 0..1024) and enable (true/false, default false; if enabled the app is started and is also started again on system restart, if disabled the app is stopped). show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> gives version, state and information per location. third-party-fw is the firmware side: show third-party-fw-<fw-name> with file-status (valid, invalid, missing), path, version, crc, vendor, part-number, nsa-upgrade-version (versions from which upgrade is non-service-affecting), present-in-eqpt and applicable-eqpt (max 80 elements each). To clear it, use clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>, which clears third party apps. If you want to act on it rather than clear it, appctl [app-name=] [command=] [[target=]] [[parameters=]] controls the app, with command restart, netls or exec, and target defaulting to system.

cli-session-config is the per-session object, and it is what you want: set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>, where cli-lines is the number of rows displayed before the output pauses (range 10..1000, default 40; press SPACEBAR to resume). It also carries cli-columns (80..4000, default 80), interactive-mode (true/false, default true, set per CLI session and not persistent) and display-timestamp (true/false, default false). cli is the management protocol as a whole: set/show cli with enabled (true/false, default true; the CLI cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port (1..65535, default 22, the ssh listener), script-dir (show only), default-interactive-mode (default true, affecting only newly created sessions) and show-alarm-columns (default default-columns, with a stated global effect on all CLI sessions). The two system-configuration objects are config and extended-config: show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)] displays the system's non-default configuration recursively from the current CLI scope, and add/delete/show extended-config-<name> configures a non-standard extended config, which introduces exceptional behavior globally and requires a name already known to the system.

set is the generic attribute assignment: set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. It needs at least one attribute-value pair, all pairs must belong to the same managed entity, and if no entity id is given the currently scoped entity is used. Wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*), ranges (card-1-[1..4]) and lists (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]) are supported, -v validates and -f forces; it prompts for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances. The separate operations are: set-alarm-state [state=]<value> [[acknowledge-text=]<value>] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]<value>...), Operational mode, which changes the operator state of an alarm to none, ack or close (state is mandatory), takes 1 up to 10 alarm ids or all-alarms, and stores an optional acknowledge-text of 0..256 characters; and set-time [new-time=]<value>, Operational mode, which changes the system time and is only applicable when time-source is manual, i.e. NTP is not enabled, with an ISO 8601 value such as 2017-01-12T10:22:25Z or +/-hh:mm instead of Z. The one that ends in -set is named-value-set: add/set/show/delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <string 1..1024>].

mc is the Media Channel, a spectrum slot on an OMS: add mc-<name> parent-oms <value> lower-frequency <value> upper-frequency <value>, with center-frequency and slot-width derived by the system (all in MHz), plus label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control and auto-delete (default disabled; when enabled the system deletes the MC once no NMC is associated, allowed on RD66TM sleds with l0-mode-op=hsc-ols and always disabled for standard or slte). nmc is the Network Media Channel, the actual carrier-bearing channel: add nmc-<name> parent-facility <value> center-frequency <value>, where parent-facility can be either a Media Channel or an OMS, center-frequency is 190650000..196700000 MHz, width is 15000..200000 MHz (default 35000, and must be set to the 3 dB signal bandwidth matching the transponder baud rate), plus attenuation targets, input-power limits and the ASE insertion attributes. For both, the referenced supporting-card must be part of a Degree, not an ADG. The fillers occupy spectrum that carries no service: mc-f (Media Channel Filler) is show-only, reporting lower-frequency, upper-frequency and slot-width; nmc-f (Network Media Channel Filler) is set/show, with admin-state and alarm-report-control settable and alloc/actual lower and upper frequency and bandwidth (alloc-bandwidth default 75000 MHz), power-actual-tx/rx and monitoring-state readable.

The scan is run by the activate command in Operational mode: activate otdr [entity=]<port> [[otdr-file-prefix=]<value>] triggers a measurement on the target OTDR port, and activate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<ots-r-id> [[otdr-file-prefix=]<value>] runs a manual OTDR-based fiber check, which executes up to 3 OTDR tests and returns an error if a manual scan or an automatic Raman fiber check is already in progress. You tune how it scans in otdr-ptp: set otdr-ptp-<name> with otdr-range (auto or 0..300.0 km; set it to fiber length plus 10%), otdr-pulse-width (auto or 10..20000 ns), otdr-measurement-speed (fast ~10 s, medium ~15 s, slow ~1 min, precision ~3-5 min, high-precision ~5-7 min, or auto, the default), otdr-ior (auto or 1.0..2.0), otdr-fiber-type (auto by default; SMF-ULL must be configured for the integrated OTDR in RD66TM and D2ILASGM and for HSC-OLS), otdr-resolution (auto or 0.4..100.0), otdr-direction-mode (default counter-prop-in-service), peak-power (auto or 5..14.5) and launching-fiber-length (0..50 m, default 0, deducted from the result). The answer comes out of otdr-ptp too: otdr-fiber-break-distance gives the distance of the break in km, or not-available if none was identified, alongside otdr-last-measurement and otdr-last-measurement-file (the .sor file). Live progress is on the otdr object: otdr-state (not-available, idle, measuring, finished, fail), otdr-measurement-time, otdr-measurement-port, otdr-measurement-direction, otdr-ongoing-measurement-profile and otdr-error. For automatic checks, ots-r-auto-otdr holds automatic-otdr, auto-otdr-state, external-attenuation-rx-measured and total-reflectance-rx-measured.

For the name server, the deciding attribute is origin on dns-server: add/set/show dns-server-<address> [origin <dhcp|manual>], default manual. origin dhcp means the address was assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and origin manual means it was configured by hand; you convert a DHCP-learned entry into a manual one by changing this attribute. What is accepted at all is governed by dns: set dns [assignment-method <manual|dhcp|both>] [enabled <true|false>] [search <string 0..64>], where assignment-method defaults to both, enabled defaults to true, and search must contain at least one dot and is cleared by setting an empty string. A deleted entry that keeps returning is a DHCP-origin entry being re-supplied while assignment-method still admits dhcp. For the relay there are two levels: dhcp-relay is global, set dhcp-relay [mode <disabled|ipv4|ipv6>] [server-address <value>], with mode defaulting to disabled and at least one IPv4 or IPv6 server address required when it is enabled; and if-dhcp-relay is per interface, set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled <true|false>, default false, and the guide states it obeys the global dhcp-relay settings. A relay that does nothing is either global mode disabled, no server-address, or dhcp-relay-enabled left false on the interface.

The wipe options live under clear [-f] system [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [[action=]<value>], Operational mode. type takes three values. factory-reset resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration; it stops target traffic services and removes the respective files and user configurations, and may imply loss of connectivity. It does not take effect for 1830 GX G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E) but is supported for the G30 controller card (FRCU), and factory-reset with the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. full-wipe cleans the entire system and reinstalls the software on the controller and the line cards, stopping all traffic services and removing all files, configurations and software; it implies loss of connectivity and needs a base software reinstall from ONIE to recover. It is not supported for G30 line cards (CHM1R, UTM2) or Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E), and is supported for the FRCU only. inactive just clears the inactive software partition. target may be the whole system or a chassis/card AID, defaulting to the entire system, and restart-behavior is restart (default) or shutdown, where shutdown means the system does not restart afterwards. The one that leaves logs and performance data behind is not a clear system option at all: clear [-f] database [[clear-type=]<full|keep-networking|initialize-from-script>] sets the NE database to default and reboots, and the guide states explicitly that it does not wipe logs, PM data and other non-configuration data.

Read show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>, which lists inventory detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a multi-chassis configuration. Per entry it gives hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (string 1..16), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and detection-timestamp, the last being the time the Node Controller last detected the unprovisioned equipment. If the slot-name is empty the entry is the chassis itself. Alongside it, show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> shows the NCT links the system has filled in dynamically, with src-chassis, dst-chassis and src-chassis-state/dst-chassis-state taking node controller, provisioned or unprovisioned, and ports on an unprovisioned chassis appearing in the form <chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>. On the chassis object itself, show chassis-<name> gives is-node-controller (true/false), chassis-role (unknown, main-chassis, sub-chassis, default unknown) and equipment-discovery-ready, which stays false until all equipment has been discovered during startup. To accept the shelf you add it with add chassis-<name> required-type <G31|G32|G34c|G42> expected-serial-number <value>, expected-serial-number being how you tell the node controller the serial number of a sub-chassis.

control-mode on the amplifier object decides it: set amplifier-<name> control-mode <auto-max-pw|manual>, default auto-max-pw, where auto-max-pw is the automatic mode targeting maximum output power and manual means you set the gain yourself. Whether auto is even offered is reported by amp-control-support (auto, meaning both manual and auto-max-pw are supported, or manual-only). In manual mode you set gain-target (0..40 dB, default 0.0) and gain-range-target (standard, low, high; default standard); gain-range-control follows control-mode automatically, going manual when control-mode is manual and auto when it is auto-max-pw. In auto mode you bias the result with gain-adjustment (-20.00..20.00 dB, default 0, only on amplifiers with function pa or inline). gain-operating reports the gain actually configured, and control-state reports the loop status (unknown, not-applicable, stopped, converged, fine-tuning, adjusting). What would stop it emitting anything: amplifier-enable is disabled by default and must be set to enabled; forced-shutdown set to true forces one amplifier of a dual-band card down; admin-state lock; and even when enabled, output power depends on the existence of the OSC signal for node-type ILA and on the OMS related facilities and the existence of an OXcon for node-type OADM. An input OLOS also triggers a shutdown after olos-shutdown-soak-timer (0..2000 ms, default 0) unless olos-shutdown-disable is true.

Which member is live is read from the protection unit: show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> [state] [role] [transport-entity]. role is working or protection, and state is active, standby, available or unknown, so the member whose state is active is the one carrying traffic. At the group level, show protection-group-<name> pg-state reports the switching state (no-request, do-not-revert, protection-lockout, frozen, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, sf-on-working, sf-on-protection, sd-on-working, sd-on-protection, wait-to-restore, unavailable, plus the -remote and exercise variants for bidirectional SNCP; default unavailable), alongside last-switch-trigger, remaining-wtr and switch-failure-reason. The behaviour on a switch is set on protection-group: protection-type (y-cable or snc-n, default y-cable), switching-mode (unidirectional, the default, or bidirectional), reversion-mode (revertive or non-revertive, default non-revertive), hold-off-timer (0..10000 ms in 1 ms steps, default 0), wtr-timer (60..720 s in 1 s steps, default 300, applicable only in revertive mode), pg-request (clear, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout, exercise; default clear), pg-control-request (freeze or clear-freeze, default clear-freeze), and the four switch triggers client-side-olos-trigger, client-side-sd-trigger, network-side-csf-trigger and network-side-sd-trigger, all enabled/disabled and defaulting to disabled. To force a switch use protection-switch [-f] operation-type=<force|lockout|manual|release> switch-target=<value> protection-group=<value>, where switch-target is not needed for release or lockout.

Trigger the check with verify [-f] type-select=fiber-connection [target-select=<port-id>] [allow-switching], Operational mode. target-select is the port instance-identifier of the CableID-capable card; if it is omitted, all paths are verified. allow-switching is boolean and defaults to false: false verifies active paths only, true also verifies inactive paths by letting the system initiate switching on the OPSM. The pre-condition is that the equipment-policies attribute cable-id-control is set to enabled. The command prompts for confirmation unless -f is used, is non-blocking, and on acceptance raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE until all queued test requests complete. Watch progress with show cable-id-status: cable-id-state is idle, running-incl-switching or running-no-switching, and test-progress is a string of the form 'N out of M completed', where M is the total number of port-pairs to be tested and N the number completed. Read the outcome with show cable-id-path-<name>, which gives card-type-a/port-a and card-type-z/port-z (CableID is sourced and terminated only by CAD10A and RD20TM and passes transparently through the OPSM), port-a-to-port-z-path-status and its reverse (enabled/disabled), the two last-test-status attributes (not-verified, pass, fail), current-state, last-test-qualifier (up-to-date or out-dated), last-test-timestamp and additional-info, which names the failure: Cable-ID TxLOS, Cable-ID RxLOS, Cable-ID-MISMATCH for a misconnected fibre, Cable-ID-RxLOF, Power out-of-range, or timeout. show -r cable-id-path-<name> adds the supporting fiber connections. show cable-id lists the CableID entities, and terminate cable-id stops all running verification tests.

Where authentication is sent is decided by security-policies aaa-authentication-method, which defaults to local-only. The remote options are local-first-then-remote (authenticate locally first, then use the remote AAA server), remote-first-then-local (use the remote server first, falling back to local if remote authentication failed or all servers could not be contacted) and remote-unavailable-then-local (use the remote server first, falling back to local only if all servers could not be contacted). If it is still local-only, no request is ever sent to the RADIUS box. The companion attribute aaa-authorization-method (local-only, local-first-then-remote, remote-if-authenticated-else-local, remote-unavailable-then-local; default local-only) governs authorization, and the user must log out and log in again for a change to apply. The server itself is add/set/show/delete aaa-server-<server-name> with protocol-supported (RADIUS, the default, or TACACSPLUS), server-address, server-priority (1..10; if not given, the lowest existing precedence plus 1), server-port (default 49), server-port-authentication (default 1812), server-port-accounting (default 1813), shared-secret (maximum 64 characters, longer values are denied with an error), source-ip, role-supported (authentication, authorization, accounting) and enabled (default true). What happens when it does not answer is governed by timeout, the response timeout for Access-Request messages, range 1..90 seconds, default 5, and retry, the number of attempted Access-Request messages to a single server before failing authentication, range 0..5; the guide notes the total wait time, timeout x (retry + 1), should be less than 5 minutes.

ssh-authorized-key holds the automation account key: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>]. Each entry is a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication; user-name is the owning local or remote user (string 0..32), key-id is a unique name for the entry (string 1..64), and public-key is the OpenSSH public key in PEM form (string 0..2048). public-key-algorithm is show-only and reports ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. For key-based login you must also set security-policies ssh-authentication-method to public-key or public-key-or-password, since the default is password. ssh-known-host holds the remote host the node trusts: add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label <value>], where address is the hostname or IPv4/IPv6 address of the allowed peer and public-key-algorithm may additionally be ssh-ed25519 (available from R9.0). How strictly that is enforced is security-policies ssh-strict-host-key-checking, strict or relaxed, default relaxed. The node's own identity is ssh-host-key: show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm> [public-key] [label] [fingerprint-algorithm] [fingerprint], one host key per supported algorithm, auto-generated in the default DB, with fingerprint-algorithm md5 or sha256. Regenerate it with ssh-keygen [-b=<key-length>] [-l=<key-label>] [-t=<rsa|ecdsa|ed25519>], default type rsa; it replaces the existing keys, and with secure-mode enabled RSA supports only 4096 bits and ECDSA 384 or 521 (default 384).

The key agreement policy lives in mka-policy, the MACsec Key Agreement policy referenced by the macsec entity on the Ethernet facility: add/set/show/delete mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority <value>] [macsec-cipher-suite <value>] [confidentiality-offset <value>] [sak-rekey-interval <value>]. key-server-priority is what the MKA protocol uses to select the key server, macsec-cipher-suite is the cipher suite for Secure Association Key (SAK) derivation, and confidentiality-offset is the number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent as unencrypted plain-text. How often the session key rolls over is sak-rekey-interval, the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range 0 or 30..65535, default 30 s. The per-port MKA instance is macsec-mka: set/show macsec-mka-<name> with mka-policy naming the policy to use, connectivity-association-key and connectivity-association-key-name (the pre-shared CAK and CKN, each string 0..64), psk-lifetime and psk-expiration-warning (range 1..173, default 14 days), psk-lifetime-enable, psk-configured-timestamp, and the read-only is-key-server. You watch the channels themselves with show sc-tx-<name>/<index> and show sc-rx-<name>/<index>, which report sci-tx or sci-rx (a 16-character hex Secure Channel Identifier), state (in-use or not-in-use, as returned by the MKA stack), association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number. The port-level object macsec-entity carries enabled, link-security-control (must-secure or should-secure, default must-secure), replay-protection, replay-protection-window (0..4294967295, default 0) and the read-only negotiated-cipher-suite.

None of them is off out of the box; enabled defaults to true on all three. netconf: set/show netconf [enabled] [port] [annotate-cli-name] [static-info-in-notifs] [hello-timeout]. port is the ssh listener for NETCONF, uint16 range 1..65535, default 830. hello-timeout is 1..3600 seconds, default 2, and the session is dropped if no hello PDU is received or transmitted in that time. annotate-cli-name defaults to false and annotates the XML output with CLI names. NETCONF cannot be disabled from within a NETCONF session. grpc: set/show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity]. The gNMI over gRPC listener port defaults to 50051, and gnmi-get-encoding-granularity is per-path or per-object, default per-object. The object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted. restconf: set/show restconf [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [cookie-timeout] [api-root]. enabled and https-enabled default to true, while http-enabled defaults to false and HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. http-port defaults to 8080 and https-port to 8181 (both 1..65535), and cookie-timeout is 1..300 minutes, default 5, reset on session activity. For reference the CLI itself listens on port 22 by default.

restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>] is Operational mode and prompts for confirmation unless -f is given. If you omit resource-id it restarts the active controller card, and if you omit type it performs a warm restart, so plain restart card-1-4 is a warm reboot. The three types are: cold, which reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, with connectivity regained within five minutes; warm, which reboots the processor of the CHM6, UCM4 and similar cards and is non service affecting, also regaining connectivity within five minutes; and shutdown, which gracefully shuts the card down. No, you cannot assume every card behaves the same way. The guide states explicitly that not all cards support all restart types, and it calls out differences: a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost, whereas a cold reboot of CHM6, UCM4 and similar is service affecting; a warm reboot of XMM4 is non-service affecting but loses visibility for 3 minutes. The restartable entities are card (cold, warm, shutdown), card sub-component (cold, warm) and tom (cold only). List the sub-components with show card resources, then restart one with, for example, restart card-1-4 DCO cold.

Three things must be in place. First, the global switch: set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <enabled|disabled>, which defaults to disabled. Application of serdes-templates depends on this flag being true; on enabling, templates are not applied retroactively, only from that moment onward, and on disabling there is no impact because the existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs regardless of how it was applied. Second, the template itself: add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <string 1..16>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>]. Templates are created per tom-part-number and apply to all line cards that support serdes; ports-applicable is a list of up to 20 port names or all, which is the default. When a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is applied automatically. Third, the actual parameter values: add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>, one entry per serdes parameter name and value, for example RxAmplitude, RxEQ, TxEQ, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor, TxEQAdaptive. The card must also support it: show supported-card-<card-type> support-serdes-config must be true, which means the card-type allows 3rd party TOM SerDes values to be configured (default false). Manual serdes configuration via add/set serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value <value> is still allowed and is kept even where it deviates from the template. Swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists, and apply-template forces re-application.

ots is the Optical Transport Section, the fibre span itself: set/show ots-<name> carries fiber-type-rx/fiber-type-tx, fiber-length-rx/fiber-length-tx (with fiber-length-derived-rx/tx), raman-coefficient-rx/tx, span-loss-reference, span-loss-transmit/span-loss-receive, span-loss-derived and span-loss-baseline, span-loss-alarm-threshold, span-loss-aging-margin-rx, external-attenuation-tx/rx, target-power-setting, target-power-adjust-cband and -lband, osc-compatibility, osc-less and osc-less-support, enable-dcn-interworking, laser-safety-mode and loading-policy. oms is the Optical Multiplex Section, the multiplexed band riding on the OTS: monitoring-mode (not-monitored, intrusive, non-intrusive, dge-fixed-attenuation, ila-with-equalization, integrated-equalization; default intrusive for all node types except ILA, not-monitored for ILA, integrated-equalization for hyperscale ILA), grid-mode (flexible by default, or fixed-50G-96ch, fixed-100G-48ch, fixed-75G-64ch, fixed-75G-64ch-oif, fixed-50G-7100, fixed-150G-40ch), lower-frequency 191300000 MHz and upper-frequency 196150000 MHz by default, band-allowed/band-actual/band-target, assigned-degree, wss-less and target-output-power (5.00..20.00 dBm, default 5). ops is the Optical Physical Section at the port: role is tributary, multi-carrier, general-purpose (default), ase-input or active-multi-carrier, with supported-roles reported by the system, input-psd-profile (-30..-6 dBm/12.5GHz, default -6) and port-expansion (no or y-cable, for Y-cable expansion). osc is the Optical Supervisory Channel and it is the one carrying the supervisory traffic: osc-mode is OC3 (155 Mbit/s) or 1GE with FEC (1.25 Gbit/s, HSC OLS nodes only), l0-comm-interface-type selects ipv4 or ipv6 for inter-NE communication, and it has osc-control (auto or manual, default auto), target-output-power (-2.5..4.5 dBm), tx-power-adjustment (-6..6 dB), voa-attenuation-target-rx (0..30 dB, default 10), osc-wavelength and lof-soak-timer (short, about 3 ms, or long, adding about 2300 ms).

The behaviour is configured on the tributary client physical termination point: set trib-ptp-<name> tributary-disable-action <value>. That attribute states what the network element does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting a replacement signal. The default is laser-shut-off, and the other values are none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (the last for 1830 GX G30 only). So by default the node turns the client laser off. You delay that with tributary-disable-holdoff-timer, the hold-off time for client shutdown or replacement signal in the egress direction, uint16 range 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 meaning the hold-off functionality is disabled; the guide notes it applies only when the TDA action is laser-turnoff, holding the optical signal as it is until the timer expires before turning the laser off. Related switches on the same object are near-end-tda (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (enabled/disabled, default disabled, for BERSD-ODU triggering ALS) and forward-defect-trigger (true/false, default true), which decides whether a received client forward defect such as LF or ODU-AIS flows through to the line side or instead triggers an egress TDA action. Example: set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off.

The super-channel comes first: the odu page states the pre-condition "Super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added", and "The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created." Every facility carries managed-by (system or user, default system) and only user-created facilities can be user deleted. The odu class attribute confirms it: high-order is the top-most ODUCn/ODUk created by the system, everything else is low-order (default) or mapped. You then hand-add the low order ODUs, e.g. add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu '1-7-L1-1-ODUCni' time-slots 1..80, with odu-type ODUCn/ODUCni/ODU4/ODU4i/ODUflexi/ODUflex/ODU0/ODU1/ODU2/ODU2e. On a G40 line side the OTU is added against the flexo-group: add otu-1-5-L1-1-OTU4-1 parent flexo-group-1-5-L1-1 time-slots 1. flexo and flexo-group also default to managed-by system.

BERT is the bert command (Operational Mode only): bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=egress test-duration=10, plus bert stop/get/delete. test-signal-type is none (default), PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV or scrambled-idles; 100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles, ODU4 uses PRBS31/PRBS31NONINV, CarrierCTP monitors fec-frames. test-duration minimum 10 s, maximum 1000 hrs, 0 means indefinite; test-id is mandatory for stop. Test patterns are injected per facility via odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> (or ethernet) test-signal-type: none, PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31, PRBS31_NONINV, with test-signal-direction ingress/egress/both and test-signal-monitoring true/false (default false). Loopback is the loopback attribute on otu, odu, ethernet and optical-carrier: none (default), facility (towards facility side) or terminal, with loopback-mode loopback or loopback-and-continue.

Each end needs a secure-entity bound to the facility and pointed at the far end: add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <facility> remote-secure-entity <AID>, where remote-secure-entity is the AID of the remote optical carrier (1830 GX G40), the remote ODU (G30) or the remote OTUFlex (CHM7/CHM7X L1 service encryption). enabled defaults to false so it must be set true; alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited; re-key-frequency is 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800; re-key-fail-policy is kill-traffic or continue-traffic (default continue-traffic) and traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s, default 0. Certificates must already be in place: a local-certificate assigned to the secure-application (set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <cert>), the far end's peer-certificate (the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for L1 encryption), and the CA trusted-certificate chain, all loaded with import-certificate.

The telemetry object configures persistent and dynamic telemetry; it is system managed and cannot be manually deleted (show telemetry, set telemetry id <string>, length 0..4096). To see what is subscribed use show subscriptions for the list, then show current-subscription-<subscription-name>, which reports related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc), session-protocol gnmi, encoding (json, bytes, proto, ascii, json-ietf; default json-ietf), transfer-mode (stream default, once, poll), updates-only (default false) and user-access. What each one watches comes from show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<path-name>: subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode (target-defined default, on-change, sample), sample-interval and heartbeat-interval in milliseconds (both default 0), and suppress-redundant (default true). For a target-defined stream with no sample-interval the system uses 10 seconds and raises a sub-10s heartbeat to 20 seconds.

At rest the database is encrypted: show db-protection-scheme reports encryption-algorithm xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 in XTS mode with 64-byte block size), integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512 or none, integrity-status passed-on-bootup / failed-on-bootup / disabled, and mode encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which is changed via the db-migrate RPC. Before take-snapshot will run, the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption must be configured, either globally with set security-policies db-passphrase or passed inline as take-snapshot db-passphrase=***. It must be a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain dictionary words, and special characters follow the 85-character Z85 set; automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. take-snapshot then stores to db-instance temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback, with an optional description up to 128 characters; show database lists what exists.

Start at the configured route: show ipv4-static-route-<prefix>/<vrf> gives next-hop-address, interface, distance (1..255, default 1), advertised (default false), origin manual or dhcp, special-next-hop blackhole, and monitoring-state (unmonitored, ok, failed) with monitoring-instance. Whether it reached the forwarding table is show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>, which lists system routes from all sources and reports source-protocol (OSPF, BGP, static) and special-next-hop none / blackhole / unreachable; for blackhole and unreachable routes no next-hop is created under the route. Which instance it landed in comes from show rib-<rib-name>, giving the vrf the RIB is bound to and its address-family, ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast; each routing instance has one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> gives the resolved next-hop-address, show vrf-<name> the VRF type (mgmt or internal), and show routing the overall view.

The rejection comes from security-policies: strict-password-check (default true) enforces minimum 8 characters, at least one lower case, one upper case, one number and one symbol, and the user name cannot be part of the password; with it disabled only a 1-character minimum applies. minimum-password-length is 1..200, default 8. enforce-password-history-check (default true) blocks reuse of any of the previous 5 passwords, with password-history-size 1..200, default 5. The lockout comes from the user object: max-invalid-login is the maximum consecutive invalid login attempts before the account is suspended, range 0..255, default 5; suspension-time is 0..1440 minutes, default 5; user-status then shows lockout, and failed-logins resets to zero on a successful login. disable-user-lockout in security-policies overrides that behaviour. To clear the stuck session run show session to find the id, then kill-session <session-id> where the id has the form <ip-address>:<port>; you cannot kill your own session.

Local log files: number-of-files defaults to 10 with a range of 1..20 retained, and when rotating on max size the oldest files are discarded once the total exceeds that number; max-file-size defaults to 30 MB, range 1..30; source-facilities defaults to all, and by default severity is set to informational and above. The default system log file cannot be edited or deleted. Console logging is off by default: log-console enabled defaults to false. Remote servers default to enabled true, port 514, transport udp, message-format rfc5424, message-coalescence true, source-facilities all, destination-facility-override disabled, sensitive-data none, origin manual. The single switch that kills everything remote is set syslog remote-logging-switch false (default true), which disables all remote logging destinations; syslog also carries log-relay (default false), log-file-message-coalescence (true), source-address (localhost), niap-compliant-logging and privacy-mode (both false).

What is raised now is show current-alarms, which gives number-of-alarms and last-changed (timestamp of the last raise or clear); show alarms or show alarm-<alarm-id> gives the detail, including perceived-severity, service-affecting, reported-time, alarm-category, corrective-action and operator-state. Manual clearing is clear [-f] alarm <alarm-type> [resource=...]; only the small subset of alarms with no automatic clear criteria can be cleared this way, and you list them with show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true. That mechanism applies only to system-wide/global alarms not associated with a particular resource. Whether inhibiting reporting drops what is already up is decided by set alarm-control arc-behavior: clear-alarms clears current alarms when ARC is set to inhibit, while leave-alarms (the default) leaves them raised. alarm-control also carries alarm-soaking-behavior, automatic (default) or no-soak.

The dashboard is status equipment, which lists chassis, the cards per chassis with their subtype, the toms per card, and per-equipment temperature sensors and power values along with presence, oper-state and alarms, for example 'chassis-1 G42 (NC) temp 25C | power 2.1/4400 W' and 'card-1-1 XMM4 (Act) temp 25C'. To narrow it to one slot's chassis pass the chassis id as the filter, e.g. status equipment 5; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so you get either all chassis or exactly one. For the raw sensor readings use show pm real-time data, which reports temperature (C) per card and per FANCTRL/PEM, inlet-temperature (C) on the chassis and fan-speed (percent) per FAN, with instant/avg/min/max columns. Physically it shows on the LEDs: show leds or show led status lists led-<location>/<name> with status off, green, flashing-green, yellow, amber, red, flashing-red, cycling (lamp test) or not-available, including entries such as led-1-2/chassis-major and led-1-FANCTRL-1/fault.

The line is the ots facility. show ots-<name> gives span-loss-derived-rx and span-loss-derived-tx, the measured span loss based on OSC including losses external to the fiber, range 0..99 dB where 99 dB means OLOS and which are only relevant when an OSC channel exists. span-loss-receive and span-loss-transmit are the user-configured fiber loss, 0..80 dB (rx also accepts 99 as not configured), default 0, and span-loss-reference selects which the system uses for automatic target OXcon powers: measured (default) or configured. span-loss-alarm-threshold (0..80 dB or 99, default 99) is set autonomously, is persistent across boots, and in measured mode can be refreshed with the update command; span-loss-aging-margin-rx is 0..10 dB, default 1.0. What the amplifier is compensating with is show amplifier-<name>: gain-operating versus gain-target (0..40 dB), gain-range-actual, input-power-mon and output-power-mon (-99..99 dBm), control-mode auto-max-pw (default) or manual, span-loss-control (default enabled, and mandatory when span-loss-reference is measured), control-state (converged, fine-tuning, adjusting, stopped) and tilt-actual.

The chain is trib-ptp, the tributary client physical termination between the transceiver equipment and the immediate protocol layer, then the client facility itself (ethernet, fc, stm or a client otu), then a low-order odu (ODU4i, ODUflexi and so on) whose parent-odu points at the high-order ODUCn/ODUCni that the system created with the super-channel. The xcon ties the two ends together, e.g. add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1, and its network-mapping attribute names the server layer that supports it. Line side you then have otu (parent flexo-group), flexo/flexo-group, and line-ptp. The digital-to-optical handover sits at line-ptp / super-channel / optical-carrier: line-ptp carries service-type and line-system-mode openwave, described as the L1 to L0 local power control adjusting Tx power from the L1 transponder towards the L0 line-system card, and optical-carrier holds frequency, tx-power, modulation-format and baud-rate. From there it is pure L0: nmc, whose parent-facility is a Media Channel or an OMS, then oxcon, oms and ots.

No, they are two different objects. Counter crossing is PM: add or set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> low-threshold <v> high-threshold <v>, where the values are uint64/int64/decimal64, na or not-supported, default na. Whether a crossing is actually reported is the separate tca-supervision flag on set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>, with per-resource-type defaults from pm-profile-entry default-tca-supervision and system limits from pm-threshold-profile. Changing how loudly an existing fault is reported is alarm severity: set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>, for example set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor, or set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>. The first creates the condition, the second re-grades a condition that already exists.

Stop the reporting with the alarm-report-control attribute: set card-<name> alarm-report-control inhibited, values allowed or inhibited. Note the card object documents its default as Inhibited, while the facilities on it (trib-ptp, odu, otu, ethernet, flexo, line-ptp, optical-carrier) default to allowed, so inhibit each facility you also want silent. You can additionally take the card out of service with set card-<name> admin-state maintenance (lock, unlock default, maintenance). What happens to the alarms it already raised is decided system-wide by set alarm-control arc-behavior: clear-alarms clears current alarms when ARC is set to inhibit, while leave-alarms, the default, leaves them raised. So on a default node the existing alarms stay up and only new ones are suppressed; set arc-behavior clear-alarms first if you want the standing alarms to drop too.

Look at the secure-application: show secure-application-<id> [type] [active-certificate-id] [in-use] [status] [verify-client-cert]. active-certificate-id is the list of certificates assigned to that application and in-use (a leafref to active-certificate-id) is the one actually presented to the far end; type shows whether it acts as server or client and status shows enabled or disabled. Assign with set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY (multiple allowed). The identity itself is a local-certificate, the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing the secure application identity; show local-certificate-<id> gives status (valid, expired, revoked, untrusted, future, pending-import), trust-chain and used-by. Before it will come up you must import it with import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=<name> <PEM string> <passphrase>, plus the CA chain as trusted-certificate (root certificates must be installed individually) and, for L1 encryption, the far end's peer-certificate. For TLS mutual authentication set verify-client-cert to required (default disabled).

Pipe the PM output through the display filter: show pm <command flag> | display csv produces CSV data importable to a spreadsheet such as Excel; display xml and display json are also available. Narrow it to the 15-minute bins with the pm-filter, for example show pm pm-15min, and filter further by AID, data-type, parameter, resource or resource-type; show pm <tab> lists every supported filter. Useful flags are -t for standard table format, -i=<chassis-name> to scope to one chassis (only once per command), -n=<number-of-records> for the maximum records per chassis (default 1000), -s=<skip-records> to page through, -st=/-et=<timestamp> in the form 2021-02-01T10:00:00+01:00, and -sbin/-ebin to bound the bins. Bin 0 is the current data and bins 1 to n are history; the NE stores 15min and 24h granularities.

Use show pm-catalog <string>, where the string is the catalog name. For example show pm-catalog parameter-undersized returns pm-parameter-undersized with units packets and type counter. The equivalent per-parameter lookup is show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type], for example show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds, and plain show pm-parameter lists all of the pm parameters. Both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. A PM parameter identifier can be either a counter or a gauge, which is exactly what the type field tells you, and units gives the measurement unit.

Turn off data-supervision on that resource: set pm-control <entity> data-supervision false, for example set pm-control pm-resource-card-1-1 data-supervision false. data-supervision is the real-time data supervision flag for the resource, values true or false, default true. show pm-control displays the configuration for all currently existing resources in the system that support PM data. The equivalent per-instance control is set pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision false, also true/false with a default of true. Both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, that is exactly what pm-control-entry is for: it configures PM for one particular resource, for one particular period, direction and location. Run set pm-control-entry-<resource>/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true, for example set pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true. direction accepts ingress, egress, all or na (default all) and location accepts all, na, near-end or far-end (default all); the same entry also carries data-supervision (true/false). show pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> supported-parameters lists the PM parameters that resource type supports for that direction and location, with a maximum of 100 elements.

Use show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]. The type field is either counter or gauge, and units is drawn from the enumeration na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors, MHz. For example show pm-parameter pm-parameter-undersized returns units packets and type counter. show pm-parameter on its own lists all pm parameters, and show pm-catalog <catalog-name> returns the same units and type pair. The parameter key is an identityref (pm parameter).

Yes: set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled. The global-data-supervision attribute exists specifically to enable PM data-supervision globally without having to toggle it individually. Its values are auto-enabled, which globally enables the PM data-supervision flag, and manual, which is the default and means the flag is controlled via pm-profile-entry or directly per pm-control-entry. The pm-profile object holds information on all resources that support PM data together with their related default configuration; it is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. show pm-profile displays the current setting. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Set the per-resource-type defaults with pm-profile-entry, which configures PM per resource type: set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision true. default-data-supervision states whether newly created resources of this type have PM data supervision automatically enabled; the companion default-tca-supervision does the same for threshold crossing supervision. Both are true/false. direction accepts ingress, egress, all or na with a default of all, and location accepts all, na, near-end or far-end with a default of all. show pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> displays the current defaults. Note that a resource created before the change is unaffected; use pm-control-entry or pm-control for those.

Use show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-data-last-reset, for example show pm-resource-trib-ptp-1-7-T9. The real-time-data-last-reset attribute is the date and time of the last real time data reset for that resource, and if the data was never reset it holds the date and time of the resource's creation. The same show also returns resource-type, AID (string, 1..64 characters) and real-time-supervision (true/false, default true), and lists the pm-control-entry children such as pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end. To perform the reset itself use clear pm real-time, optionally narrowed by resource, resource-type, period, direction, location or AID.

Create a pm-threshold keyed on that exact instance: add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/errored-seconds high-threshold <value>, for example a key of the form <resource>/pm-15min/ingress/near-end/errored-seconds. The same key works with set to change it, show to read it back and delete to remove it. low-threshold and high-threshold accept a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), na for not applicable, or not-supported, and both default to na. direction accepts ingress, egress, all or na with a default of all; location accepts all, na, near-end or far-end with a default of all; period is the PM period, for example pm-15min or pm-24h. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use pm-threshold-profile, which holds the PM configuration per parameter for a resource type: show pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> [low-threshold] [high-threshold] [default-low-threshold] [default-high-threshold] [min-value] [max-value]. default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold are the system defined default values for that parameter, while min-value and max-value are the minimum and maximum values the parameter allows, so they bound what you may configure; low-threshold and high-threshold show what is currently configured. All six accept a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), na, or not-supported. You write a new limit with set, for example set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200.

Use the clock command (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). Set the zone with 'set clock timezone <value>', for example 'set clock timezone Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00]'. The value comes from the fixed named list (International Date Line West[GMT-12:00] through Kiritimati[GMT+14:00] plus Universal-Time-Coordinated); the default is Universal-Time-Coordinated.
