The add command for super-channel-group works in merge mode only, so -m is required in the documented syntax: add -m super-channel-group-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <lock|unlock|maintenance>] [auto-in-service-enabled <value>] [valid-signal-time <value>] [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>] [line-system-mode <value>] [openwave-contention-check <value>]. Using -m performs a best-effort add: if the target entity does not exist it is created, and if it already exists it is updated with whatever attributes are present on the add command. Defaults on that object: admin-state unlock, alarm-report-control allowed, auto-in-service-enabled false, line-system-mode openwave, valid-signal-time 480 minutes (range 1..7200), managed-by user.

Use show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> [capacity] [client-mode] [baud-rate] [application] [compatibility-id] [status] [supported-subtypes], in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. carrier-mode is an acronymized handle for the optical carrier line mode 4-tuple, a string of length 1...15, formatted <Capacity><ClientMode>.<Baud Rate><Application ID>; examples are 600E.84P, 100X.73U and 325M.66P. capacity is the net capacity of the optical carrier in gbps, so that is the field giving what each mode yields. client-mode is the digital client mode mapped into and transported by the superchannel's carriers, ethernet or ethernet-otn. baud-rate is the modulated symbol rate. application is the optical transport application ID the mode is optimized for, string 1...15. compatibility-id identifies which carrier modes can be applied simultaneously, and status gives the state of the carrier mode. supported-subtypes lists the subtypes each carrier mode supports, string length 0..32 with a maximum of 20 elements.

Use show supported-gain-range-<name>/<gain-range-type> [gain-range-min] [gain-range-max], available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. gain-range-type selects which range you are asking about and takes low, high or standard. gain-range-min returns the minimum settable gain-target for that type of range ('standard'/'low'/'high') and gain-range-max returns the maximum settable gain-target for it; both are of type gain-value, and the guide gives no fixed numbers because they are reported per entity. So query the object for each of the three gain-range-type values to get the actual settable gain-target window that each of low, standard and high represents.

A card type can support several power profiles because they reflect different scenarios in which the card is used. You choose, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice changes the power estimation for the system. Inspect them with show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. card-type and name (the profile name) are strings and are the two keys. profile-description is a string of length 0...255 explaining the profile. power-draw is a decimal64 giving the power draw of the associated equipment when it is not in low-power, and this is the value that drives the estimation. default is true or false, indicating whether that profile is the default one for the card type.

It comes from the router-id-mode attribute of the bgp-instance. router-id-mode takes use-loopback or manual and defaults to use-loopback, meaning the router ID is taken from the loopback IP unless you switch to manual. When you want to set it explicitly, supply the router-id attribute, an IPv4 or IPv6 address; 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6. The syntax is add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>], and both fields can be changed later with set bgp-instance-<instance-id>. instance-id is a string of length 1...255 and local-as is a number in the range 1 .. 4294967295. Example from the guide: add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback

On bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address> the timer defaults are: connect-retry-interval 120 seconds (range 1..65535), the interval between attempts to establish a session; hold-time 90 seconds (range 3..65535), the time a session is considered active without keepalives, typically 3x the keepalive-interval; and keepalive-interval 30 seconds (range 1..21845), typically 1/3 of the hold-time. show also returns negotiated-hold-time (range 0..65535 seconds, default 0). Yes, you can authenticate the session: secure-session sets the authentication method to none or TCP-MD5 and defaults to none, and password carries the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII format, a string of 0..80 characters. All of these are settable on add and set. Related: peer-as is a number 1 .. 4294967295, enabled defaults to true, and session-state is shown as Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established or Close.

The route has to be in the forwarding table already. The routes to be advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. For routes that are not present in the IGP tables you must configure blackhole static routes: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole (special-next-hop takes the value blackhole on both ipv4-static-route and ipv6-static-route, on add and set). Also check the bgp-network object itself exists for the prefix: add bgp-network-<instance id>/<remote-address>/<network prefix>, where instance-id is a string 1...255, remote-address is the BGP peer in IPv4 or IPv6 format (0.0.0.0/0 and 0::0.0 are not supported), and network-prefix is a decimal number 1..64 or 128. A maximum of 100 bgp-network MOs can be configured.

mtu on comm-channel is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, an integer (uint16). The range depends on the platform: 1280..1500 octets on 1830 GX G30 only, and 1280..9202 octets on 1830 GX G40 only. The default is 1500, except that on 1830 GX G40 the following interface types default to 1518: DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4. The parameter is available only when the mode is L3 (mode takes L1, L2 or L3 and defaults to L3). mtu can be given on add -m comm-channel-<name> and on set comm-channel-<name>, and read with show. The related receive-side value, mru, is an integer in the range 64..1500 octets with default 1500, also only available in L3 mode. Example: add comm-channel-gcc0 type GCC0 label GCC0 alarm-report-control allowed mtu 1500 parent otu-1-6-1-OTUC4

LLDP is off by default: lldp-admin-status on comm-eth defaults to disabled, and its values are tx-only (transmits but does not store remote system information), rx-only (receives but does not transmit), tx-and-rx and disabled. It cannot be modified if the mode is L1. Turn it on with, for example, set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. lldp-transmit-interval is 1..16383 seconds with a default of 30 seconds, and lldp-mgmt-addr-if selects which interface's IP is advertised as the management address (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only), L0-MGMT); it is empty by default, falling back to the loopback IP, then to the DCN/AUX IP. For speed: auto-negotiation defaults to enabled, so the ports negotiate. rate is only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled, takes 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum and defaults to maximum; duplex-mode defaults to full; flow-control defaults to disabled; mtu is 1280..1500 octets, default 1500.

Use the global dhcp-relay object: set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>], readable with show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]. Both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. mode is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, defaulting to disabled. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses, IPv4 or IPv6; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Examples from the guide: set dhcp-relay mode ipv4, and set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3. This is the global setting only; to actually run the relay on a given interface, set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true, which obeys these global dhcp-relay settings.

Yes. The dns object has an assignment-method attribute that indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values; the assignment method can be both manual and dhcp. Its values are manual, dhcp and both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts DHCP-supplied name servers alongside the ones you configure. Set it with set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and read it with show dns; both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The other attributes are enabled, a flag for whether DNS is enabled, true or false with default true, and search, the DNS-search-suffix name, a string of length 0..64 that must contain at least a single dot and is cleared by setting it to an empty string. Per-server origin is tracked separately on dns-server.

Add one with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server and is the key; delete dns-server-<address> removes it, set dns-server-<address> origin <value> changes it, and show dns-server-<address> [origin] displays it. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The origin attribute is the DNS address assignment method and is how you tell where an entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that has been assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the DNS address has been manually configured. The default is manual. You can also convert a DHCP-configured DNS entry into a manually configured one simply by changing this attribute. Example from the guide: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp

Use the if-dhcp-relay object, which is per interface: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>], and read it back with show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. Both are available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string of length 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface; its values are true and false and the default is false. It obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global dhcp-relay mode must be ipv4 or ipv6 (it defaults to disabled) and a server-address configured for the relay to do anything. Examples from the guide: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true and show if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled

By default it is statically addressed and protected. On add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> ..., ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and both default to static; ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled are true or false and both default to true, so both stacks are connected unless you disable one. protection-mode takes unknown, protected or unprotected and defaults to protected (protected means protected by redundant ports, unprotected means no port redundancy, unknown is a transient output-only state); the read-only protection-state reports the current state and defaults to unknown. Other defaults: admin-state unlock (lock, unlock, maintenance), alarm-report-control allowed, oper-state disabled, proxy-arp-enabled false (only applicable to the DCN interface), and if-dhcp-relay false. if-type is ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp or hdlc. Note a static IPv4 address cannot be added when DHCP is enabled on the interface.

Yes, that is what ip-monitoring does: a monitoring instance periodically pings a destination and the result takes action on configured static routes. Create it with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is taken when monitoring goes into 'failed' state; it takes none or withdraw and defaults to withdraw, so the route is pulled by default. static-route is the list of connected static routes for the instance, maximum 10 elements. destination is the remote host to monitor (IPv4 or IPv6); next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address, and the instance is not active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is 0...60 seconds, default 5. drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1. enabled is true or false, default true. The route's monitoring-state then reads unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>, in Operational or Candidate Configuration Mode. There is a pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string 0..64 characters; type ? after ipv4-address- to list the available interfaces. Three address classes are disallowed: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), addresses beginning with 127 (loopback), and addresses beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). netmask must be a valid netmask. show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] displays it, where origin is static, dhcp or auto-config with default static, and delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> removes it. Examples: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0' and add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0

distance is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, and it defaults to 1. It is set on add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. For a discard route, use special-next-hop, whose only value is blackhole (usable on add and set). Blackhole static routes are required for routes that must be advertised to an external AS but are not present in the IGP tables, since routes advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself. Other defaults: advertised is true/false defaulting to false (when true the route is advertised in the routing protocol; for OSPF it is advertised as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR), and origin is manual or dhcp defaulting to manual. Example: add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165

It is the same shape but the subnet is expressed as a prefix length, not a netmask: add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, with show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin] and delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. There is a platform note: an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. if-name is a string 0..64 characters; type ? after ipv6-address- to list available interfaces. origin is read-only in show and takes static, dhcp or auto-config with default static. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64

Yes. Give the interface parameter the value DCN-B on add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. The guide notes that static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. The interface named must be bound to a VRF matching the vrf given in the route key. Example from the guide: add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B, alongside the DCN form add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN. Defaults on the route: distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual (or dhcp), and special-next-hop blackhole for discard routes.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. It retrieves management address information about a particular chassis component; multiple management addresses may be configured on the remote system whose information is received on the local system, each with a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). The keys are lldp-port, the local port connected to this LLDP neighbor (an instance); direction, ingress or egress; address-subtype, the identifier encoding used in address (string); and address, the string 0..64 used to contact the management entity. if-subtype describes the basis of the interface associated with the address and takes unknown, if-index or system-port-number; if-id is the integer interface number; address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity, a string 0..128.

They carry the same attribute set but differ in scope and key. management-address is keyed show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>, including a direction key of ingress or egress, and covers addresses received on the local system from the remote system. management-address-local is keyed show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> with no direction component, and is used to view the management address information from the local LLDP ports (show management-address-local lists them all). Both are show-only, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and both return if-subtype (unknown, if-index based on the ifIndex MIB object, or system-port-number based on the system port numbering convention), if-id as an integer, and address-oid as a string 0..128; on management-address-local the address-oid field is currently an empty string.

Yes, it is the use-as-source attribute of the networking object: set networking [use-as-source <value>] and show networking [use-as-source], both available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. use-as-source names the interface to use as the source address and takes a string of length 0..64; the guide lists no default value for it. Example from the guide: set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, with show networking to view the current networking information. use-as-source is the only parameter on the networking command.

show networking-services. That is the whole syntax; the command takes no parameters and is used to show the list of network services. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The guide's example is simply show networking-services. It is a show-only command, with no add, set or delete form.

Because the next-hop list is a child of the RIB, not of a bare route. In `show next-hop`, each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family. For each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family, so a next hop is only meaningful inside the RIB (and therefore the address family) it was resolved in. The syntax reflects that: `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]`, where rib-name is a String of length 1..64 with pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*), destination-prefix is an IP prefix, interface is the outgoing interface name (for example DCN) and next-hop-address is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Example: `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`. Bare `show next-hop` lists all entries. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration.

Use `clear [-f] ospf [instance=]<value>`. The command removes and restarts an ospf-instance, and the operation is asynchronous, so the CLI does not wait for the restart to finish. The instance id is supplied as <instance> and is a string; there is no default. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation, otherwise you are prompted. Access mode is Operational Mode only. Example: `clear ospf 1`. The ospf-instance itself is created and removed with `add ospf-instance-<instance-id>` / `delete ospf-instance-<instance-id>`; `clear ospf` is the asynchronous restart path referenced from the ospf-instance section.

No. The `ospf-area` commands are `add|set|show ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type <value>]` and `delete ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>`, and the only permitted value of ospf-area-type is `normal`, which is also the default. Stub and NSSA area types are not offered. instance-id is uint8 in the range 0..255 and ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `add ospf-area-1/0.0.0.0`.

Use `ospf-area-range`, which summarises routes for an OSPF area matching address/mask. It is applicable to Area Border Routers (ABRs) only, so it has no effect on a non-ABR. Syntax: `add|set ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix> [advertise <value>]`, plus show and delete on the same AID. The advertise attribute takes true or false (advertise or hide) and defaults to true. prefix is an IPv4 prefix (length <= 32) or IPv6 prefix (length <= 128) in canonical form, with all non-prefix bits zero. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `add ospf-area-range-1/9.9.9.9/10.220.0.0/16 advertise true`.

Yes. `add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <value> [version <value>] [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>]` accepts version `ospfv2` or `ospfv3`, with ospfv2 as the default. instance-id is uint8 in range 0..255 and description is a String of length 0..128. The router id is controlled by router-id-mode, which takes `manual` or `use-loopback` and defaults to use-loopback; with manual you supply router-id as a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: if router-id-mode is use-loopback, an IPv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. `show ospf-instance-<instance-id>` can also display vrf. Examples: `add ospf-instance-1 description abc router-id-mode manual version ospfv2 router-id 100.100.1.1` and `add ospf-instance-2 description xyz router-id-mode use-loopback version ospfv3`.

On `ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>` the defaults are hello-interval 10 seconds (uint16, range 1..32767) and router-dead-interval 40 seconds (uint16, range 4..65535). Related timers: retransmission-interval default 5 seconds (2..3600) and transmit-delay default 1 second (1..450). ospf-cost defaults to 10 (1..65535) and priority to 1 (0..255). Authentication is available: ospf-auth-enable is true/false, default false, and is only relevant for ospfv2 or ospfv3; ospf-auth-algorithm takes none or HMAC_SHA_256, default HMAC_SHA_256, and ospf-auth-key is an ASCII string of length 0..256, both only relevant for ospfv2. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance and OSPF area must exist before adding the interface.

Use `show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id> [state] [role] [address] [priority]` in Operational Mode. The states are: down (initial, no Hello packets received), init (Hellos received but bidirectional communication not established), 2-way (bidirectional established, DR/BDR election occurs here), exstart (DR and BDR elected, master-slave relation determined), exchange (neighbors exchange DataBaseDescriptor packets containing LSA headers), loading (routers exchange full Link State information based on DBDs) and full (full adjacency achieved). The role values are drother (Designated Router Other), dr (Designated Router), bdr (Backup Designated Router) and ptp (point-to-point). Note that an OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down. priority 0 means the router is not eligible to become DR or BDR.

Add a security association with `add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> integrity-algorithm <value> [ipsec-protocol <value>] [ipsec-mode <value>]`, with matching set, show and delete forms. The spi is a unique uint32 in the range 256..4294967295. integrity-algorithm is mandatory on add and takes AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 or AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96, with no default. ipsec-protocol supports only ESP (default ESP) and ipsec-mode supports only transport (default transport). Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: `add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 integrity-algorithm AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128`.

Use `ping [-c=<count>] [-w=<timeout>] [-s=<pktsize>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <ping-dest>`. -i=<interface> specifies the source interface; by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF; by default the MGMT VRF is used. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. -c stops after sending count ECHO_REQUEST packets, -w sets a timeout in seconds after which ping exits regardless of packets sent or received, and -s sets the number of octets sent exclusive of headers, default 56 plus 8 octets of ICMP header for a total packet size of 64 octets. ping-dest may be an ipv4-address, ipv6-address or domain-name. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: `ping -c=1 -w=10 -s=1024 192.0.2.3`.

Use `show protocols [ssh|cli|serial-console|netconf|grpc|snmp|restconf|http-file-server|data-model-openconfig]`. With no argument it lists all nine: ssh, cli, serial-console, netconf, restconf, grpc, snmp, http-file-server and data-model-openconfig. Adding one of the keywords shows that protocol's attributes, for example `show protocols ssh` gives enabled, port (8022 in the sample), host keys and pre/post-login messages; cli shows enabled, port 22 and script-dir /storage/scripts; netconf shows enabled, port 830 and annotate-cli-name; restconf shows http-enabled, https-enabled, http-port 8080, https-port 8181, cookie-timeout and api-root /restconf; grpc port 50051; snmp port 161 plus snmp-engine-id; http-file-server http-port 8980, https-port 8981, url-base /transfer; serial-console global-switch and global-timeout. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]`. Each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB for each supported address family. rib-name is a String of length 1..64, vrf is a leafref to ../../vrf/name showing the VRF the RIB is bound to, and address-family takes ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `show rib-IPv4` views the RIB identified by the IPv4 key.

Use `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]`, which shows the list of system routes from various sources such as dynamic protocols and static route. The source-protocol attribute gives the source protocol for the route entry, for example OSPF, BGP or static. rib-name is a String of length 1..64 and destination-prefix is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. special-next-hop is also available: it applies to IPv4 and IPv6 static routes, rib:routes and IP Monitoring, and takes none (no special treatment, used for all normal routes), blackhole or unreachable, with none as the default; for blackhole and unreachable routes no next-hop is created under the route. Plain `show route` lists all system routes. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes: `show routing`. It shows routing information and takes no parameters at all. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the level of detail below it, use the related commands on the same node: `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]` for the per-address-family RIBs, `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]` for the routes themselves, `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]` for next hops, and `show vrf-<name>` for the routing instances.

`show supporting-interface-<name>/<interface>` shows supporting interface information, that is, which underlying IPv4/IPv6 interface backs a given interface. It has two parameters: name, the name of the interface, a string; and interface, a reference to the IPv4/IPv6 interface, given as the path ../../../../../networking/interface/if-name. Both are used only in show. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

`traceroute [-m=<hopcnt>] [-w=<timeout>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <tr-dest> [pktsize]` probes a maximum of 30 hops by default; -m sets the maximum number of hops (max time-to-live), uint8 in range 1..255. The VRF defaults to MGMT: -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF and if not provided it defaults to MGMT. -i=<interface> sets the source interface, and by default the interface is selected according to the routing table; -i and -v are mutually exclusive. -w is the timeout in seconds before traceroute exits, uint16 range 1..10, default 2. pktsize is the total probing packet size, default 60 (60 bytes for IPv4). tr-dest may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain-name. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: `traceroute -m=10 -w=3 1.2.3.4`.

Use `show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description]`, which shows the Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instance. chassis-name gives the chassis associated with that VRF. name is a String of length 0..32, description is a String of length 0..255 describing the VRF and its intended purpose, and type is either mgmt (Management VRF) or internal (Internal VRF). Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: `show vrf-MGMT` views the Management VRF attributes; plain `show vrf` lists the instances.

Use `activate [-f] swimage [label <string>] [db-action <empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback|auto>]` in Operational Mode. A successful swimage activation implies a system restart. The optional db-action parameter specifies what happens to the database: auto (default) activates the image processing the database with the system default behaviour, empty-db activates with an empty database, upgrade-db activates by upgrading the current database, and rollback rolls back to the previous active software image. If db-action is not provided the system decides automatically. Unless the -f option is given, you must confirm the activation when prompted; -v forces the validate check again. label specifies the sw image/manifest file name, and if not specified the currently installable image is used. Example: `activate swimage db-action=empty-db`.

No: only a single location led test can be running at a time, so you cannot flash two cards simultaneously. The command is `activate location-led [entity=]<value> [[timeout=]<value>] [[led-mode=]<value>]`, where entity is a chassis or a card (for example `activate location-led card-1-1`). led-mode is flash (default), an amber light blinking at 1 Hz used for LED location, or solid, a steady amber light used for lamp test, which lights all chassis LEDs amber. To turn it off, use `terminate location-led <entity>`; invoking it when no test is active has no effect. Alternatively set timeout, a number in the range 0..120 seconds, default 0, which means no timeout so the function runs until terminated. Note the timeout parameter does not take effect in 1830 GX G30 R5.1, and not all cards support the location LED test.

Use `bootstrap ([local-port=]<value> | [neighbor-address=]<value>) [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-password=]<value>`. It bootstraps a neighbor NE by establishing a TLS connection over the OSC link and provisioning the initial administrator account on that neighbor, for commissioning an OSC peer that has no configured users yet. Select the neighbor either with local-port, the supporting-port of an osc-eth MGMT interface as shown by `show interface` (for example 1-1-dwdm-line1), or with neighbor-address, the IPv6 link-local address of the OSC peer including zone (string length 7..256, pattern 'fe80:.*'). With local-port the system maps it to the OCE netdev OCE-<chassis>-<slot>-<vlan-id> and resolves the peer address via get_osc_neighbors.sh; if resolution fails the RPC is rejected. new-admin-user is mandatory, length 1..32, and follows local user naming rules; new-password may be plain text (standard complexity rules apply) or a $6$ SHA512 hash. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Type `cancel-upgrade`. The full syntax is `cancel-upgrade [-h]`, where -h just displays help for the command; there are no other parameters, flags or arguments. It cancels any active upgrade in progress. Access mode is Operational mode, and the stated pre-condition is that an upgrade must be in progress for the command to execute successfully, so it will not succeed on an idle node. The example given is simply `cancel-upgrade`. To see the versions being installed and their installation status, use `show upgrade-status`.

`change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]enabled` starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, so on an in-service node you lose the configuration and the node restarts. The ztp-mode parameter takes enabled or disabled and has no default; -f forces the command without confirmation, so without it you are prompted. `change-ztp-mode disabled` disables ZTP and will stop ZTP if it is already in progress; the command can be executed while ZTP is running, interrupting it. Access mode is Operational mode. Display the current ZTP mode configuration with `show ztp`. Example: `change-ztp-mode disabled`.

Use `show current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name> [fw-version] [expected-fw-version] [fw-status]` (equivalent forms exist for <card-name>.<slot-name>, <chassis-name>-<slot-name> and <name>). Compare fw-version, the current version of the firmware, against expected-fw-version, both Strings of length 0..32. fw-status states it directly and takes current (current firmware is up-to-date), not-current (current firmware is not up-to-date against the expected one) or unavailable (information on firmware status is currently unavailable), with unavailable as the default. Example: `show current-fw-1-3/DCO_1`, or plain `show current-fw` for the whole node, which prints rows such as current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT 0x20 0x28 not-current. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

`download` accepts these filetypes: crl (a CRL in PEM format), database (a previously uploaded database), file (any file to the file-system), krp (key replacement package), local-certificate (PKCS#12 with password-protected private key, or PKCS#7 if pending-import), peer-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#12), script (a CLI script), swimage (downloads a manifest file then all files belonging to the SW image) and trusted-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#7 Root or Intermediate CA). The system automatically stores the downloaded file in an appropriate place; there is no need to provide a local location. Only filetype file takes a destination, which may be omitted (default directory, original name), a file-name, a relative path or an absolute path, and you need write access to it; use `show transfer` to see the default storage directory. A downloaded database is stored as a db-instance=temp database, overwriting any existing temp. Access mode: Operational mode.

Use `show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature]`, which retrieves information about downloaded image files. manifest-file is the downloaded manifest file and its information, a String of length 0..256; name is the name of the downloaded software image, a String of length 0..256; and signature is the downloaded software image file signature, a String of length 0..1024. Plain `show downloaded-image` lists all downloaded software image files. Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

`show downloads` shows the list of downloads. It takes no parameters, and its access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands cover the detail: `show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature]` retrieves information about downloaded image files, `show transfer-status` reports the progress of an asynchronous transfer started with `download -a`, and `show sw-management` shows information about software locations, activity and downloads.

Yes, but only within your own access rights. The `file` command (Operational mode) does basic file and directory operations: `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>`. The permitted operations are rename, view (listing for a file or directory), delete, sha256sum and md5sum. new-file-path is only used with rename. The guide states that file system access is restricted to the current user's access, so not all files/directories are editable. A `result` attribute reports the file operation result. Examples: `file rename /tmp/a.log /tmp/b.log`, `file view /tmp`, `file delete /tmp/a.log`, `file sha256sum /tmp/a.log`. For system-managed files use `clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>` with filetype krp, script or swimage; swimage only deletes a downloaded image not yet installed, and krp needs no target-file since only one may exist. `show file <filename>` displays a file's contents.

Both run in Operational mode and both are described as performing basic file and directory operations, but `file` is the fuller command. `file-operation [[operation=]<value>] [new-file-path=]<value> [file-path=]<value>` supports only three operations: rename, delete and view. `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>` supports rename, view, delete plus the two checksum operations sha256sum and md5sum, and it exposes a `result` attribute holding the file operation result. The `file` entity also carries the related forms `show file <filename>` to display a file's contents and `clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>` to remove a krp, script or swimage from the system. In both commands new-file-path is only meaningful for rename.

Use `add file-server-<name> server-address <value> protocol <value> [server-port <value>] [user-name <value>] [password <value>] [initial-path <value>] [label <value>]`, with matching set/show/delete forms and `show file-servers`. Access is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. protocol accepts file, ftp, sftp, scp, http and https; `file` means local storage including USB and requires initial-path to be provided. ftp and http are applicable only when secure-mode is false. server-address may be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address or a domain name. server-port is optional: if omitted, the default port for the selected protocol is used. name is a string 0..64 characters, user-name 0..64, password 0..128, initial-path 0..256, label 0..256. Example: `add file-server-139 server-address '10.220.227.139' protocol 'scp' user-name 'root' password 'Nokia' initial-path '/root'`.

Use the file-type command: `show filetype-<name> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [last-operation]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `name` is the file type for which the transfer happened. last-completion-status gives the last transfer status, last-transfer is the last transfer start timestamp as a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (see the set-time command), last-duration is the last transfer duration as a time-interval, and last-operation reports whether it was an upload or a download, or unknown. For richer per-operation detail including progress, bytes and session, use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation>` instead; transfer status only exists if at least one operation of that kind has been done for the filetype.

Yes, but it is off by default. `set http-file-server [enabled <value>] [http-enabled <value>] [https-enabled <value>] [http-port <value>] [https-port <value>]` and `show http-file-server [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [url-base]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `enabled` is the master switch for file server access and defaults to true. `http-enabled` defaults to false and `https-enabled` defaults to true, so only HTTPS is on out of the box; set http-enabled true to allow plain HTTP. The default http-port is 8980 and the default https-port is 8981, both user configurable numbers. `url-base` is read-only in show and defaults to /transfer (string, 1..100 characters); it is the base URL used to redirect to the file transfer application.

Use the manifest commands, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information]` gives the manifest itself: its signature (hex-string, 0..1024), the downloaded timestamp in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ format, and an information string (0..256). `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]` lists each package it contains, where state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), version is 0..64 characters and description 0..512. `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` shows the firmware carried per equipment-type. manifest-file is 0..256 characters, equipment-type and fw-name 0..32, name 1..256. `show manifest` lists all manifests.

No. The packaged-fw command explicitly states that versions for the same firmware can be different per equipment-type within one software-load. Query it with `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` or, without a location, `show packaged-fw-<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`; `show packaged-fw` lists all of them. Access is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id>, a string up to 64 characters. swload-state is active, inactive or installable. equipment-type is the card or other equipment type that will use the firmware (0..32 characters), fw-name is the firmware name (0..32) and fw-version is the included version (0..32). Example entries look like packaged-fw-active/CHM6/DCO-OEC and packaged-fw-active/XMM4/IOP.

Yes. `prepare-upgrade` has two options: validate, which validates the software label/manifest, and apply, which applies it. Syntax: `prepare-upgrade [-f] [-i] [-u] [option=]<value> [manifest=]<value> [[db-action=]<value>] [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>`, Operational mode. Flags: -h help, -i ignore validation failures, -u unattended (auto-activate software after prepare-upgrade apply), -f force without confirmation. db-action is valid for unattended upgrade only and takes empty-db, upgrade-db or rollback, defaulting to upgrade-db. clear-type (only valid for an unattended operation with db-action empty-db) takes full, keep-networking or initialize-from-script, defaulting to full; keep-networking and initialize-from-script require new-admin-user and new-admin-password, and initialize-from-script also requires script (a .cli file). Example: `prepare-upgrade validate -f G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188.manifest`, then `prepare-upgrade apply -f <manifest>`.

`clear [-f] recover-mode` clears the recover-mode flag. Per the guide, this clears the current recover-mode state of the NE, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring the traffic settings. Because of that reconfiguration it may be traffic impacting. The command runs in Operational mode and has no parameters; the only flag is -f, which forces the command without the confirmation prompt. Use `clear recover-mode` to be prompted for confirmation, or `clear -f recover-mode` to skip it.

Use `show software-load-<swload-state>` or, per location, `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. swload-state is active (active software load), inactive, or installable (the load waiting to be used). Readable attributes are swload-version (0..64), swload-manifest (0..256, only relevant for installable), swload-prepared (true/false, only relevant for installable), swload-status, swload-information (0..1024), swload-activation-type (direct = no reboot type determined, warmstart = warm reboot required, coldstart = cold reboot required; only relevant for installable), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. swload-status runs through status-unknown, validate-in-progress/complete/failed, apply-in-progress/complete/failed, activate-in-progress/complete/failed, cancel-in-progress/complete/failed, plus validate-timeout, apply-timeout, activate-timeout and cancel-timeout. Example: `show software-load-active` or `show software-load-1-5/active`.

Use `show software-location-<location-id>`, where location-id is the equipment location as <chassis-id>-<slot-id> (string 0..64). It runs in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. For example, `show software-location-1-5` retrieves software location information for the card in chassis 1, slot 5. To drill into a particular load on that slot, use `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>`, for example `show software-load-1-5/active`, with swload-state active, inactive or installable. The same view is reachable from the umbrella command as `show sw-management software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable]`, for example `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`. Component detail per slot comes from `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>`.

Use `show subtype-constraint-<card-type>/<subtype> [min-capacity] [max-capacity] [supported-applications] [unsupported-applications] [description]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. card-type and subtype each represent a group of related PONs for a card type to which the constraints apply, and are strings of 1..20 characters. min-capacity is the minimum capacity supported by the subtype and max-capacity the maximum, both in gbps; a max-capacity of -1 means there is no maximum capacity constraint. supported-applications lists the application types the subtype supports and unsupported-applications lists those it does not; if either list is empty, that constraint is not applicable. description is a string of 1..255 characters.

Use `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, or `show sw-component-<swload-state>/<name> ...` without a location; `show sw-component` lists them all. Access is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The `state` attribute is the answer: installed (software package installed), not-installed, installation-failed (software package install failed) or unknown, with unknown as the default. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> (0..64), swload-state is active, inactive or installable, name is the package name (0..256), version is 0..64 and description 0..512. Example: `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`. For finer granularity drop to `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`, which reports the same state values per subcomponent.

Use `show sw-container-<container-name> [equipment] [state] [description] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode; `show sw-container` lists all OS-level containers. cpu-usage is the container's current CPU usage as a number in the range 0..100 percent, and on a multi-core system it indicates the overall usage relative to all cores. memory-usage is the current memory usage as a percentage in the range 0..100. state is off (default, not launched yet), up (running) or exited. equipment is a leafref to the card AID the container runs on, and uptime is the time since the container started. Example: `show sw-container-frcu31-1-5_pyapi`. Per-service rather than per-container figures come from `show sw-services` / `show sw-service-<sv-name>`, which also expose cpu-usage and memory-usage.

Yes. sw-control-rule adds service-specific custom rules that override the default action on service failure. Use `add sw-control-rule-<service-name> fail-action <value>`, `set sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action <value>]`, `show sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action]` and `delete sw-control-rule-<service-name>`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. service-name is the name of the service to be monitored, a string of 0..64 characters. fail-action takes three values: default-action, which performs the policy of restarting the service and then rebooting the system if the service does not recover; ignore, meaning no automatic action is taken on service failure; and system-restart, which performs a warm restart of the system/card software immediately upon service failure. Example: `add sw-control-rule-xmm4-1-1_host_KeyManagement fail-action default-action`.

Yes, `show sw-management` is the umbrella view of software locations, activity and downloads, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Syntax: `show sw-management [downloads | software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable] | software-load-active | software-load-inactive]`. `show sw-management downloads` lists the download history, that is the downloaded manifest files. `show sw-management software-load-active` and `... software-load-inactive` show the node-level active and inactive loads, listing their sw-component and packaged-fw entries plus swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label. `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active` narrows the same view to one shelf and slot.

Use `show sw-service-<sv-name> [equipment] [location] [state] [state-details] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime] [last-start-time] [reboot-count]`, or `show sw-services` for everything, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. reboot-count is the number of times a service has restarted, a uint16. Pair it with last-start-time, the time of the last service start/boot as a date-time in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ format, and uptime, the time since the service turned up expressed in days:hours:minutes. state is off (not being monitored), ok (ready and functional) or fail (failed to launch/turn-up or unresponsive), with state-details giving a brief description. sv-name is the unique service instance id containing card type, shelf and slot, for example `show sw-service-frcu31-1-5_host_DpEncrMgr`. To change what happens on repeated failure, use sw-control-rule fail-action.

sw-subcomponent goes one level deeper than sw-component: it keys on the subcomponent inside a package rather than the package itself. Syntax: `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> [state] [version] [description]`, or without a location `show sw-subcomponent-<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> ...`; `show sw-subcomponent` lists all. sw-component by contrast keys on <location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>. The reported attributes are identical: state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown, default unknown), version (0..64) and description (0..512), with swload-state being active, inactive or installable and component/subcomponent names 1..256 characters. Example: `show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb` versus `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`. Access is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Type `swversion`. It retrieves the active, inactive and/or installable versions of the software present on the network element, takes no parameters, and runs in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The output lists one line per load with its version and label, at node level and per slot, for example: software-load-active R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188; software-load-inactive R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.04.15_14_26-sim-112; software-load-installable R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188; then software-load-1-1/active, software-load-1-1/inactive and software-load-1-1/installable for the card in chassis 1 slot 1. For the same information with more attributes use `show software-load-active` or `show sw-management software-load-active`.

Use `show third-party-fw-<fw-name> [file-status] [path] [version] [crc] [vendor] [part-number] [nsa-upgrade-version] [present-in-eqpt] [applicable-eqpt]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. file-status is the firmware file status and takes valid, invalid or missing. crc is the cyclic redundancy check of the firmware image, used to validate the file when present. path is the path for the firmware image (0..255) and version, vendor and part-number are strings of 0..64. applicable-eqpt is the list of resources this firmware can be applied to and present-in-eqpt the list of resources that already contain this version; both lists have max-elements 80. nsa-upgrade-version (0..255) states the versions from which the upgrade is non service affecting.

Set it on the transfer entity: `set transfer [http-proxy <value>]`, read it back with `show transfer [debug-log-optional-content] [http-proxy]`. Access is Operational or Candidate configuration mode. http-proxy is the proxy server for internally-generated HTTP requests leaving the NE, which includes certificate revocation-related requests, that is CRL downloads and OCSP requests. Note the important restriction: this proxy is not used for file transfers. The value is a string of 0..1024 characters in the format '[http://]<host>[:<port>]', where 'http://' is optional, <host> may be the IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS name of the proxy server, and <port> is optional; if <port> is omitted the default is 1080. Example: `set transfer http-proxy http://1.2.3.4:1080`.

Use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [transfer-type] [session-id] [session-user-name] [filename] [transfer-progress] [bytes-transferred] [total-bytes] [details]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode; `show transfer-status` shows every entry. operation is upload or download. transfer-progress is the completion percentage, 0-100, default 0; bytes-transferred and total-bytes are uint64 byte counts, both default 0, and total-bytes stays zero until it is known at transfer start. details gives the transfer phase: completed, Failed, idle, preparation or transfer, default idle. last-completion-status is a string such as success, fail, in-progress or unknown; unknown can occur if the system reboots while a transfer is in progress. transfer-type is sync or async. In synchronous mode a textual progress bar is rendered live in the CLI; asynchronous transfers (-a on download/upload) are tracked with this command. A transfer-status entry only exists once an operation of that kind has been done for the filetype.

Use `show upgrade-status-<resource> [to-swload-version] [status] [start-time] [end-time] [step] [step-start-time] [details]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The status is reported at NE level, chassis level and card level; `resource` (string 0..255) selects the object, and for ne and chassis the results are aggregated summaries of all cards in that scope, so start at the NE and drill down to the failing card. status values are idle, upgrade-in-progress, upgrade-complete, upgrade-partially-failed, upgrade-failed, validate-in-progress, validate-failed, validate-complete, apply-in-progress, apply-failed, apply-complete, activate-in-progress, activate-failed, activate-complete, cancel-in-progress, cancel-complete, cancel-failed and no-communication, with idle as the default. `step` is the identifier for the current upgrade step (0..128) and step-start-time when it was initiated. start-time and end-time are the current phase's timestamps and show 'na' if the entity has been idle since startup or has not finished a phase. to-swload-version is the target load and details (0..255) carries the explanation.

Use `upload [-a] [-s] [filetype=]<value> ([destination=]<value> | [file-server=]<value> [[path=]<value>]) ...` in Operational mode with filetype=debug-log, which uploads logs for diagnostic troubleshooting and includes all other logs. debug-entity is a mandatory parameter for debug-log and targets a specific chassis or card; if absent all data is included. optional-content adds keyword-selected extra content (see `show transfer debug-log-optional-content`). Example: `upload debug-log destination=scp://user@someserver//home/user` produces a name like debug_log_GX_11-18-11-2020-19.07.48.tar.gz. Certificates are different: for filetype local-certificate, peer-certificate or trusted-certificate you must give certificate-name (1..128 chars), except for trusted-certificate where omitting it exports all trusted certificates as a bundle. Only the public part is exported, private keys are not, and the output files are in P7 pem format. -a uploads asynchronously (track with `show transfer-status`), -s skips TLS or ssh known-host verification.

Use `show ztp [ztp-mode] [ztp-state] [ztp-details] [ztp-completion-status]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. ztp-mode is the user-set mode, disabled or enabled, default enabled; it is set via the change-ztp-mode RPC, which is allowed even when the NBI is locked. ztp-state is the current state of the ZTP service and progresses through ztp-init (the default), dhcp-in-progress, image-download-in-progress, image-install-in-progress, custom-script-execution-in-progress, multi-chassis-setup-in-progress, configuration-apply-in-progress, ztp-completed, plus ztp-state-unknown, ztp-disabled and wait-before-ztp-restart. ztp-details is a string of up to 256 characters giving additional information on the current state. ztp-completion-status summarizes completion for the node as not-completed (default) or completed.

Use the capabilities command: 'show capabilities-<name>', where <name> is the name of the card (string). It retrieves the capability information for that one card. It is a show-only command, available in both Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. 'name' is the command's only parameter and has no default (n/a). For example, 'show capabilities-1-4' returns the capabilities of the card named 1-4. For type-level (rather than instance-level) capability data, the related commands are supported-card, supported-port, supported-slot and supported-tom.

Provision with 'add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name <value>', so the three mandatory attributes are required-type, chassis-name and slot-name. required-type is the card type, a String of length 0..32, taken from the supported list (BAXOFP2, BLANK, BLANK2, CAD10A, CDC8D6, CHM1R, CHM2T, CHM6, CHM7, CHM7X, FAN, FAN-CTRL, FRCU, ILAx, IOPANEL, OCC2E, OCC2T, OMD32E, OMD64, PEM, RD09SM, RD12TI, RD20TM, RD32TH, RD66TM, RPBL, RPBM, SPN2, SPN2C, UCM4, UTM2, XMM4 and others). chassis-name is a String 1...255 with default 1; slot-name is a String. Optional on add: required-subtype, card-mode, subslot-name (settable only at creation), power-profile, alias-name, admin-state (default unlock), alarm-report-control (default inhibited), label. Example: 'add card-1-4 required-type CHM1R chassis-name 1 slot-name 2'.

On the 1830 GX G40 you must set the chassis ambient temperature to 40C before a Native ZR TOM will come up. If configured-ambient-temperature is not set, the system raises a port config mismatch alarm and the TOM cannot be provisioned. Use 'set chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature 40' (the attribute is a number in Celsius units, has no default, and is available on add, set and show). Its stated purpose is to be used to compute the FRU's power consumption. Once the chassis ambient temperature is configured, provision the pluggable normally.

Use 'set console-<name> baud-rate <value>' / 'show console-<name> [baud-rate] [actual-baud-rate] [auto-sensing-state]'. Permitted values are auto-sensing, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200. The default is 9600 in 1830 GX G30 and 115200 in 1830 GX G40. Yes, it can work it out itself: in auto-sensing mode the system auto-detects the baud rate from 'ENTER' presses on the serial console client side, then locks the detected rate, which is reported in actual-baud-rate. auto-sensing-state shows sensing or locked (default sensing) and is only visible if auto-sensing is enabled for the port. Not all cards support auto-sensing; supported-card console-port-support reports no, yes-with-auto-sensing-baud-rate or yes-with-fixed-baud-rate.

Use 'show controller-card-<name> [redundancy-status] [redundancy-standby-status] [number-of-switchover-events] [time-of-last-switchover] [additional-details]'. redundancy-standby-status is the attribute to check: ready-synchronized means the standby controller is in sync and ready; other values are not-ready-synchronizing (synchronizing data with the active controller), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out (protection in lock-out state) and card-not-present. The default is not-ready-synchronizing. redundancy-status reports active, standby or not-in-service (default not-in-service). number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover are only visible on the active controller card; additional-details is a string up to 128 chars giving further synchronization status. Example: 'show controller-card-1-12'.

Use 'show equipment [<option>]', which displays installed equipment information; the available options vary according to your installation. With no option it lists the installed equipment; with an option it narrows the output to one item, for example 'show equipment card-1-1'. That returns the card's child objects (controller-card-1-1, console-1-1, port-1-1-AUX-1, port-1-1-AUX-2, port-1-1-CRAFT, port-1-1-DCN, port-1-1-U1) plus attributes such as required-type XMM4, required-subtype, category controller, chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, alias-name, AID, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state, alarm-report-control and label. It is a show-only command, valid in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes for pluggable subtype, via 'set equipment-policies tom-auto-migration enabled|disabled'. That enables automatic update of the TOM subtype based on the present equipment; it may directly impact existing configurations, and it covers subtype migration only, not TOM type migration (there is no update between QSFPDD and QSFP28). Degrees are governed separately by auto-assigned-degrees (enabled, disabled), which enables automatic degree assignment when a card that supports degrees is provisioned; its default is disabled, except enabled if l0-mode-op is hsc-ols. The related auto-assigned-directions is enabled by default. Read current settings with 'show equipment-policies'.

You have to enable them. 'set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <value>' controls whether serdes-templates are globally enabled; the values are enabled and disabled (the CLI value completion offers false and true), and the default is disabled. On enabling, templates are not applied retroactively: they will be applied from that moment onward. On disabling there is no impact; the existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs, whether it was applied via template or manually. Check the setting with 'show equipment-templates use-serdes-templates'. Application of serdes-templates depends on this flag being true, and you can force re-application with the apply-template command.

Use 'show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>'. It displays the packaged FRU information associated with a particular equipment-type. manifest-file is the manifest file, a string of length 0..256; equipment-type is the type of the equipment, a string of length 0..32. Both parameters have no default (n/a) and the command is show-only, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the data of an actually installed FRU (serial number, CLEI, part number, dates), use the inventory command instead.

Use the inventory command, which shows inventory data for a present FRU: 'show inventory-<name>', or addressed as 'show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>', 'show inventory-<card-name>.<slot-name>' or 'show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>'. serial-number is the serial number of the equipment (String) and clei is the Common Language Equipment Identifier (String). The same command also returns hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision (Number, default 0), PON, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and insertion-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ or 'NA'), number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code (0...18 chars, for 3rd party TOMs), actual-power-class (uint8 1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status (not-applicable, current, not-current, unavailable; default not-applicable). Example: 'show inventory-1-3-1'.

Use 'show led-<location>/<name> [status]' or 'show leds'. location is the AID of the equipment location of the LED (chassis, card or port AID; 1..32 chars) and name is the LED name within the FRU (1..16 chars). The status values are: not-available (status not available), off, yellow, flashing-yellow, green, flashing-green, red, flashing-red, cycling-with-off (cycling between all supported colors including off), cycling (cycling between all supported colors excluding off, used for lamp test), amber and flashing-amber. The default is not-available. Yes, the object exists even if the FRU is not physically present; in that case the status typically reads not-available. Example: 'show led-1-1/active' returns 'status green'.

In 1830 GX G40 there are three kinds of port: comm-eth, USB and trib/line. comm-eth and USB ports are on XMMs only and are found on Slot 1 XMMs. The trib/line ports can be seen on a CHM6 or a CHM7 (slots 4-7) only after a TOM is present/provisioned in the CHM6/CHM7. Port objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. The port-type attribute shown by 'show port-<card-name>-<port-name> port-type' takes: line (line-side colored CWDM/DWDM module), tributary (grey client interfaces), tributary-subport (a tributary split into subports), usb, comm, uplink (aggregation ports to an adjunct line function), optical, otdr, pluggable (the L0 module cage for a QSFP/SFP/SFP+ TOM) and ocm.

Use 'show resources-<name> [internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth] [internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth] [paired-slot-total-bandwidth] [paired-slot-available-bandwidth]'. The internal-cell-switch attributes apply only to SPN2/SPN2C cards and default to 600.000 Gbit/s if the card has paired slot interconnection capability. The paired-slot attributes apply only to SPN2/SPN2C cards that support Paired Slots: they default to 0 if the card has no paired slot interconnection capability, and to 500.000 Gbit/s if it does. The same command also returns supported-carriers, unassigned-carriers and supported-sub-components. Example output for 'show resources-254-1': internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth 600.000 Gbit/s, internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth 358.750 Gbit/s, paired-slot-total-bandwidth 500.000 Gbit/s, paired-slot-available-bandwidth 258.750 Gbit/s.

Read the status attribute: 'show serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> [value] [status]'. status is the state of the advanced parameter as observable on the system once it is configured, and takes: set (parameter set), unknown (parameter unknown), in-progress (parameter in progress), failed (parameter failed) and not-supported (parameter not supported). The default is unknown. So the parameter has taken effect when status reads set. Example output of 'show serdes': serdes-1-7-T1/RxAmplitude value 1 status set, serdes-1-7-T1/TxEQ value 1 status set, serdes-2-6-T2/RxEQ value 3 status set. The value itself is set with 'add|set serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value <value>'.

A serdes-template is keyed by TOM part-number, created with 'add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <value>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>]'. tom-part-number is a string of length 1..16 and is the part-number the template applies to; when a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is applied automatically. Templates apply to all line cards that support serdes. Port scope is set by ports-applicable: 'all' if all ports are to be considered (the default behaviour), or a list of port names, each a string of length 1..16, up to a maximum of 20 elements (for example T1..T16). Manual serdes configuration is still kept even if it deviates from the template. Swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template, if one exists. Application depends on use-serdes-templates being true; apply-template forces re-application.

Each entry is one serdes parameter name plus its value, added under the template: 'add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>'. Edit with 'set serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> [value <value>]', remove with the delete form, and view with 'show serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name>/<name> [value]'. name is the name of the serdes parameter, a string of length 0....256, and value is the value of the serdes parameter, a string of length 0...256; the template is identified by tom-part-number, a string of length 1..16. Examples: 'add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3' and 'set serdes-template-entry-TR-FC85S-NIN/TxEQ value 2'. Typical entry names are RxAmplitude, RxEQ, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor, TxEQ and TxEQAdaptive.

Yes. The serial-console object holds the global configuration of all serial console ports in the system: 'set serial-console [global-switch <value>] [global-timeout <value>]' and 'show serial-console [global-switch] [global-timeout]'. global-switch allows access by serial console and takes enabled or disabled, with default enabled; each console port can override this global behaviour (the per-card console attribute local-switch takes use-global-switch, force-enable or force-disable, defaulting to use-global-switch). global-timeout is the serial console inactivity timeout, a number in minutes, default 60, and can be set to zero to disable the inactivity timer. The object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: 'set serial-console global-switch enabled global-timeout 80'.

Use 'show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> [AID] [supported-type] [installed-type] [oper-state] [avail-state] [current-equipment]' (or 'show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>' for a subslot); 'show slot' lists every slot. current-equipment is the name of the equipment currently required in this slot (for example 1-1), and shows --- when there is none. supported-type is the list of types the holder supports (for example CHM6,gx:UCM4) and installed-type is the type currently installed, empty when no FRU is present. oper-state is enabled or disabled (default disabled) and avail-state carries values such as normal in-service or partially-faulted abnormal in-service. For the full type-level slot capability, including possible-card-types and requires-blank-when-empty, use supported-slot.

Use 'show sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name> [AID] [description]'; running 'show sub-component' with no key lists them all. card-name is the name of the card supporting the sub-component (string, 0..64 characters), sub-component-name is the name of the sub-component (string), AID is the Resource Access Identifier (string, 1..64 characters) and description is a user configurable description of the sub-component (string, 0..128). It is show-only, in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example output: sub-component-1-6/dco-oec with AID 1-6-dco-oec and description 'DCO OEC (Optical Engine Controller) sub-component', and sub-component-1-6/dco-secproc with AID 1-6-dco-secproc. The card's own list of addressable sub-components is also reported by 'show resources-<name> supported-sub-components'.

Use 'show supported-card-<card-type> node-type-compatibility'. node-type-compatibility gives the supported NE node-type for a sled card and is only of relevance for line-cards and carrier-cards. The values are: all (compatibility with any node-type), ILA (compatibility with the In-Line Amplifier, two-directions node type) and OADM (Optical Add/Drop Multiplexer node type). So a card is usable on an in-line amplifier node if it reports all or ILA. The same command also reports sw-support-revision, supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode, supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. Example: 'show supported-card-CHM1R'.

Use 'show supported-chassis-<chassis-type> [controller-redundancy-supported] [number-of-front-slots] [number-of-rear-slots]'; chassis-type is an identityref such as G31, G32, G34c or G42. controller-redundancy-supported is true or false and states whether that chassis supports controller redundancy. number-of-front-slots is the number of equipment holder slots in the front plate and number-of-rear-slots the number in the back plate, both uint8. It also reports supported-subtype, default-subtype, description, power-control-supported, fan-adjustment-on-altitude (default false), dust-filter-replacement (not-applicable, optional-dust-filter, dust-filter-regularly-replaced; default optional-dust-filter), depth in mm, height in RUs, leds and supported-subchassis-type (max 10 elements, empty means no multi-chassis support). Example: G42 reports controller-redundancy-supported true, 7 front slots and 12 rear slots.

Use 'show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name> [port-type] [direction] [configuration-mode] [faceplate-label] [leds] [present] [default-tom] [parent-port] [subport-list] [allows-auto-migration]'. port-type says what the port is for: line, tributary, tributary-subport, usb, comm, uplink, optical, otdr, pluggable or ocm. configuration-mode says who configures it: system-configured means the system automatically configures the card in the slot (or TOM in the port) and the user cannot make changes; user-configured means the user can provision or de-provision. present is always or in-node-controller-only (default always), and allows-auto-migration (true/false, default true) indicates whether TOMs plugged on this port type are auto migrated per the equipment-policies tom-auto-migration flag. Example: 'show supported-port-CHM1R/2'.

Use 'show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name> [possible-card-types] [requires-blank-when-empty] ...'. requires-blank-when-empty states whether the slot needs a BLANK filler card when empty and takes not-applicable, optional or required. possible-card-types is the list of card types allowed in that slot, with a maximum of 15 elements. The command also returns slot-location (front or rear), slot-vertical-position and slot-horizontal-position (uint8), configuration-mode (system-configured or user-configured), auto-provision-capable (true/false), default-card, reset-power (card reset power consumption at 55C in W), virtual-slot (default false) and leds (max 10 elements). On a G42, for example, slots 1, 3, 4-7 and PEM-1..PEM-4 are required, while slot 2, the FAN slots and FANCTRL-1 are not-applicable; slots 4-7 list possible-card-types CHM6,UCM4.

Use 'show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> [supported-subtype] [supported-phy-modes] [default-phy-mode]'. It reports TOM capability in the scope of a particular card and port. tom-type is the form factor (for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28, QSFPDD) and tom-subtype-group is a string of 0..32 characters such as '4x100GE-breakout'. supported-phy-mode lists the phy-modes supported in that TOM on that card and default-phy-mode the one used by default; the values are 100GE, 200GE, 400GE, 2x100GE, 4x100GE, 100G, 4x10G, 4x10GE, 1GE, 2G5, 10G, 10GE, 2G5E, 40GE, 40G, 4x100G and 200G. supported-subtype lists the subtypes allowed for that TOM type in that card/port. Examples: 'show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFP28' and 'show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFPDD/2x100GE-breakout'.

Use 'show supported-tom-power-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type> [supported-power-class] [supported-max-power-draw]'. tom-type is the pluggable form factor (TOM type identity), matching the TOM required-type, for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28 or QSFPDD. supported-power-class is the maximum MSA power class the host port supports for that pluggable type, a uint8 in the range 1..8; the port may only partially support that class, so read supported-max-power-draw as well, which is the maximum power in watts (decimal64) the host port allows for that pluggable type under supported-power-class. What the fitted module actually reports is on the inventory side: actual-power-class (uint8 1..8) and actual-max-power-draw, populated only for third-party transceiver subtypes on hosts that enforce power-class rules, not for native qualified subtypes.

Yes. When you create a TOM with 'add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>', the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created along with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. required-type is mandatory on add and takes CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS. Optional attributes on add/set are required-subtype (string 0..32), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label, enable-serdes (false/true, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; CHM7 cards only). Example: add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD

Use 'show tom-type-<tom-type> [data-rate] [description] [support-third-party-toms] [generic-subtype]'. The support-third-party-toms attribute is a boolean (false/true) that says whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to the supported Nokia TOMs. The companion attribute generic-subtype gives the 3rd party subtype string for that TOM, data-rate gives the approximate rate as uint16 in Gbps, and description is a human readable string (0..255). 'show tom-type' with no AID lists all supported types. The command runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related: on the TOM itself, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled) exists specifically to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

It shows up under 'show unprovisioned-inventory', which lists detected inventory that the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration has not yet accepted.
