The AID form is unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>; chassis-serial-number is a string 0..16 and slot-name is a string 0..16, left empty when the equipment is the chassis itself. Retrievable attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (string 1..16), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ format, and detection-timestamp, which is the last time the Node Controller detected that unprovisioned equipment. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Run 'show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]', for example 'show usb-1-5-U1'; plain 'show usb' lists every USB port in the node with its type and present state. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted, a string 0..32, and it can be used as the target or source for file transfer operations. available-space is the current free space and total-space the total space, both uint16 in MB. All three of usb-path, available-space and total-space apply only when type is storage; the other role is power-supply, which powers external equipment such as passive shelves. present (true/false, default false) indicates whether the connector is inserted.

Use 'activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]' from Operational mode. db-instance names the snapshot to activate and defaults to temp; paraphrase is a short description of the database being activated, a string of length 40...200; sanity-check-override takes true or false and defaults to false, and is used to override the sanity check. The stated pre-condition is that a snapshot must already have been taken, with the related take-snapshot command. Examples given are 'activate-snapshot sanity-check-override' and 'activate-snapshot onehour'. Existing snapshots can be listed with 'show database'.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after 'enable-advanced-parameters' on the optical carrier is set to true. Two documented behaviours explain what you are seeing: if no advanced parameter is configured, or the advanced parameter was deleted, 'show advanced-parameter' reports 'ERROR: object does not exist'; and if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value the configuration is not rejected, but 'show advanced-parameter' reports status 'failed' for it. The AID is advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name>, with add/set/show/delete. status values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set and unknown, default unknown.

Use 'apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*])' in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Set template-type to serdes-template, which applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOM list given in applicable-tom; if you do not supply applicable-tom, all system TOMs are considered for template application. Example: 'apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1'. This matters because 'set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates enabled' does not retroactively apply templates: on enabling, templates are applied only from that moment onward, so apply-template is how you push them onto already-installed pluggables. Disabling use-serdes-templates has no impact; existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs.

Yes, use a confirmed commit. From Candidate Configuration mode, entered with 'configure', run 'commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]'. The candidate configuration is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not occur before the timeout elapses, the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version, so the confirmation acts as a persist trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. You confirm with 'commit persist' and abort with 'commit cancel'. For a Persistent Confirmed Commit the commands must carry the -id parameter, which ties commit confirmed, commit persist and commit cancel together. 'commit -m=<message>' attaches a custom message to a commit.

Use 'show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]' and pipe it through the display command: 'show config | display commands', then store the result for later use. That is the documented way to create a CLI script that can restore the system configuration. 'show config' displays only non-default configuration, skipping anything left at its default value, and the output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. To narrow the scope, supply an entity-id (the instance ID of one entity) or an entity-type when all entities of that type are relevant.

It depends on the target you pick. 'configure <target>' takes exclusive or shared, and defaults to exclusive. In exclusive mode only your session can make changes to the candidate configuration; in shared mode multiple sessions can change it concurrently. The command runs from Operational mode and moves you into Candidate Configuration mode. By default the candidate datastore starts as a copy of the running datastore, but you can change the starting point with 'from-default' for a blank config from scratch, 'from-script=<script>' to import configuration from a text file of CLI commands, or 'from-commit=<commit-id>' to initialize from a past commit record. from-commit is only available when the Commit Repository feature is available, that is when the commit-tracking system-policy is enabled. Example: configure exclusive

Use 'show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]', which shows the current values of the advanced parameters actually running on the system, as opposed to 'show advanced-parameter', which reports what you configured plus its status. Plain 'show current-advanced-parameter' lists them all; a wildcard form such as 'show current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/*' limits output to one optical carrier. Attributes are optical-carrier-name and current-advanced-parameter-name, both strings, and value, a string holding the running value. Typical entries include BOASetting, CRAvgNCtrl, ClockPreEmphasis, EEPNNLMitigation, FastCDAcqTimeCtrl, NLC, PDLMitigation, RxCDCompCtrl, RxCDMode and TxSignalBWControl. Note that PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. 'clear [-f] database' performs a full wipe of the database contents, sets the NE database to default and reboots the system, and is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity to the system. It does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data; use the 'clear system' command when you need a secure wipe or factory default. clear-type takes full (reset to factory defaults, the default), keep-networking (full wipe but network configurations are kept) or initialize-from-script (full wipe then initialize from a pre-stored .cli script). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user and new-admin-password and can only be triggered by the SA user. Expect transient alarms after the controller card reboot; these should be ignored. -f forces the command without confirmation.

Run 'db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>' from Operational mode with type set to encryption-with-integrity; the other permitted value is encryption. The example given is 'db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity', which enables the integrity check for the system database and automatically reboots the controller. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. The resulting protection scheme is visible with 'show db-protection-scheme', whose mode attribute reads encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and is documented as changeable via the db-migrate RPC. With integrity enabled the integrity-algorithm becomes hmac-sha2-512 rather than none, and integrity-status moves off disabled.

Run 'show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode]' in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode and read integrity-status, which reports passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled. The other attributes are encryption-algorithm, which is xts-aes-256-plain64, AES-256 encryption in XTS mode with 64-byte block size; integrity-algorithm, either hmac-sha2-512 or none; and mode, the current protection scheme of the DB, either encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which can be changed via the db-migrate RPC. On a node that has not been migrated the output reads integrity-algorithm none, integrity-status disabled, mode encryption-only.

Use 'diff [-t|-c] candidate', which must be run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists the differences between the candidate datastore and the current system configuration as created, deleted or changed objects, showing only configurable attributes; 'new' data is the candidate and 'old' data is the current system configuration. Output forms: default normal diff style, where + marks added objects or new values and - marks deleted objects or old values; -t for a side-by-side table diff; -c to render the changes as CLI commands that reproduce the same configuration; and -d to list the commands being executed. So yes, 'diff -c candidate' gives you commands. 'diff commit <id> [<id>]' compares a commit record against the running configuration or another commit record, and is available when commit-tracking is enabled or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run 'discard-changes' from Candidate Configuration mode. It discards all candidate datastore content and returns the CLI to operational mode. The command takes no parameters and no flags. Its access mode is Candidate Configuration mode only.

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, so treat it with care. It requires that you already know the extended-config name, and the name must match a name known by the system. The commands are 'add extended-config-<name>', 'delete extended-config-<name>' and 'show extended-config-<name> [description]', usable in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. name is a string of length 0..64. Before adding one, read the description attribute, a string of length 0..255 supplied by the system, which states what the extended-config is and its effect in the system.

Check the service-impact attribute in the Golden Advanced Parameter Table with 'show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> [description] [type] [supported-values] [direction] [multiplicity] [configuration-impact] [service-impact]'. service-impact is read-only and reads service-affecting or non-service-affecting; if it is service-affecting you must perform an admin lock or maintenance operation, or other relevant operations, before applying the change. configuration-impact identifies the configuration steps needed to apply the change: no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change or full-config-no-pll-change. Also read supported-values for the allowed ranges or discrete numbers, multiplicity for how many values you must enter, and direction (transmit, receive, transmit-and-receive). Example: show golden-advanced-parameter-chm7/EEPNNLMitigation

Run 'lock' (flag -h shows help) from Operational mode. It locks database access to the current session and grants that session exclusive write access, intended for holding configuration mastership for a short time. While the database is locked, any other session, CLI or otherwise, that tries to make a configuration change receives an error, and a lock is not possible if another session already holds one. The lock is released either by 'unlock' or by the locking session closing, whether the user closes it explicitly, an administrator closes it, or it hits the inactivity time-out. Only the session that took the lock can unlock it; unlocking a non-locked database, or one locked by another session, fails. After the unlock any session can configure again or take a new lock.

A named-value-set is addressed as named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>, where db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for that set. It holds a single 'value' item, a string of length 1..1024 characters. The commands are 'add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>]', 'set ... [value <value>]', 'show ... [value]' and 'delete ...'. All four are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

That depends on the restore-from-chassis-storage setting, shown and changed with 'show recovery' and 'set recovery restore-from-chassis-storage <value>'. Values are disabled (chassis storage is not used for restoration on this NE), auto-restore (SW and DB are stored on chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, then a manual clear recovery-mode is required, which lets you validate the restored system before affecting the HW), and auto-in-service (SW and DB are restored in recovery mode and on successful restore the NC automatically leaves recovery mode). The default is auto-in-service, so with defaults it does pick the configuration up by itself. 'show recovery' also reports restore-status (init, image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade, wait-for-db-restore), backup-status (successful, failed, in-progress, unknown), last-backup and next-backup.

Only if the candidate is empty. 'rollback commit [<commit-id>]' works in the Running Datastore by default or in the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if it is empty, which is in fact a way to initialize the candidate. If you omit the commit-id, the most recent commit record is used. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse commands for each record, and replays them in order from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit record. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

'show commit' is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. If neither holds on your node, there is no Commit Repository to visualize. Turn it on with 'set system-policies commit-tracking enabled'; the default for commit-tracking is disabled. Note that disabling the policy again clears the commit-repository of all commit records. The syntax is 'show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>]', where <id> selects one specific commit record, -s picks a timestamp and shows all records created since it, and -n selects an exact number of records. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'set system-policies [commit-tracking <value>] [writable-running <value>]' and 'show system-policies [commit-tracking] [writable-running]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. commit-tracking enables the commit-repository feature, so all configuration changes made through the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit records that can be visualized, compared and rolled back; values enabled or disabled, default disabled. Disabling it clears the commit-repository of all commit records. writable-running is also enabled/disabled with default disabled; disabling the writable-running policy makes it impossible to configure via the running datastore, forcing use of the candidate: CLI allows add/set/delete only in Candidate mode, NETCONF allows edit-config only via the candidate, and RESTCONF, gNMI (telemetry still allowed, gNOI still allowed), WebGUI and TL1 all become read-only.

The db-passphrase is missing. The system only accepts 'take-snapshot' if the db-passphrase used for DB snapshot encryption is configured, either globally as part of security-policies with 'set security-policies db-passphrase', or locally as a parameter, for example 'take-snapshot db-passphrase=***'. The passphrase needs a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and may use special characters from the 85-character Z85 set. Automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Syntax is 'take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]' from Operational mode. db-instance takes temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; description is a string 0...128. Re-taking an existing instance overwrites the existing file.

Use the `template` command. A template is a single template entry defined by an object/attribute pair plus the value to be used as the default for that attribute. Syntax: `add template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> object <value> attribute <value> value <value> [sequence-id <value>] [label <value>] [condition <value>]`, with matching `set`, `show` and `delete template-<template-group-name>/<template-name>`. `object` is the object name to apply to (for example odu), `attribute` the attribute name (for example admin-state), and `value` is the value to apply and is mandatory (for example lock). `sequence-id` is a Number in range 1..65535 that defines the processing order, lower ids first. `label` and `condition` (for example service-type=OTU4) are optional. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `add template-1/FansInMaintenance object card attribute admin-state value maintenance condition card-type=FAN`.

No. On `template-group` the `enabled` attribute takes true or false, and its default is documented as true only if there is no other template-group enabled. So a newly added group comes up enabled only when no other template-group is already enabled; one enabled group at a time is the model. The commands are `add template-group-<name> [enabled <value>] [label <value>]`, `show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label]` and `delete template-group-<name>`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The group is a configuration group containing a list of template entries; `label` is an optional string. Example: `add template-group-1` adds and enables the group.

Use `show templates`. It shows the configuration that defines the data model for system templates, that is the overall view of templates on the node. The command takes no parameters and is available in both Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the level below it, `show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label]` shows an individual template group, and `show template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> [sequence-id] [object] [attribute] [value] [label] [condition]` shows an individual template entry.

No. `unlock` releases a database previously locked with `lock`, but only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock. If a session tries to unlock a database that was locked by another session, or a database that is not locked at all, the `unlock` command will fail. The lock is released automatically if the session that performed the lock is closed, so the lock will clear once that session ends. Syntax is `unlock [-h]`, where -h displays help, and the access mode is Operational Mode. After the unlock any session is able to perform configurations and to perform a new lock.

Yes, use `validate candidate <candidate> command <string>`. It validates the contents of the specified configuration, that is any CLI command used to edit a configuration datastore by creating, deleting, merging or replacing content, without applying it. `candidate` is the candidate datastore targeted for validation and `command` is the command to validate; both are strings with no default. If the command is validated the command replies with OK, otherwise the command fails. Multiple CLI commands can be provided in one call if they are separated with ';'. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `validate 'set ne altitude 600'`.

A maximum of 7 rounds of `additional-key-exchange` can be configured; the additional-key-exchange-id is 1..7 and you must choose a unique key-exchange algorithm for each round. The rounds must be configured in the same order on both IKE peers; if the configuration does not match, an IKE-CONFIG-MISMATCH alarm is raised. Configuring additional-key-exchange also causes the IKE session to go down immediately and renegotiate the new proposal. Syntax: `add additional-key-exchange-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<additional-key-exchange-id> dh-group <value>`. dh-group values are dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512, ml-kem-768, ml-kem-1024. Configuration is optional; Child SA (port level) key exchange is derived from IKE. For PQC safety configure PPK or at least one post-quantum algorithm, ml-kem-1024 recommended.

Use `show data-path-encryption`. It shows the datapath encryption attributes. The command takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related global policy for L1 datapath encryption is set with `set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <match|ignore>`, and on-demand re-keying of a datapath encryption secure entity is done with `re-key secure-entity=<value>`.

Ciphers and key lengths are keys of the `encryption-algorithm` object, so you name them in the AID: `add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>` for an IKE SA proposal, or `add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>` under an SPD entry. `algorithm` values are null, aes-gcm-8, aes-gcm-12, aes-gcm-16, aes-ctr, aes-cbc, aes-ccm-8, aes-ccm-12, aes-ccm-16, chacha20-poly1305. `key-length` values are none, key-length-128, key-length-192, key-length-256, default none. `number` is the proposal number for the IKE SA, range 1..max. Only add, show and delete are supported, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `add encryption-algorithm-ipsec/GX2/1/aes-gcm-8/key-length-192`.

On `add ike-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>` you must supply `integrity-algorithm` and `dh-group`; `prf` is optional. integrity-algorithm values: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512. prf values: hmac-sha2-256, hmac-sha2-384, hmac-sha2-512, hmac-sha1. `number` is the proposal number for the IKE SA, range 1..max. `protocol-id` is show-only and is always IKE. Access mode Operational and Candidate Configuration. Example: `add ike-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/1 dh-group dhe-2048 prf hmac-sha2-256 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-384-192`.

The top-level `ikev2` object carries a single attribute, `data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match`. It is a global, L1 encryption-specific policy indicating whether the NE must validate the certificate Subject Alternate Name to match the IKE ID (OPT-IN) or not (OPT-OUT). Permitted values are match and ignore, with no default stated. Syntax: `set ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <value>]` and `show ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match]`, in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match match`.

Use `show ikev2-local-instance-<name> host-card-encryption-capability`; it indicates whether the card on which this IKEv2 local instance is running supports the ability to do encryption, with values yes, no, unknown and default unknown. `host-card` is a read-only reference to the service card running the instance. For the address, `local-address-assignment-method` is show-only with values auto and manual, default auto; `local-address` is the local IPv4 address for the IKEv2 channel with prefix-length 32, default 0.0.0.0, and is settable. Other attributes: `scope` (data-path-encryption, management-ipsec, local-address, local-address-assignment-method), `admin-state` (lock, maintenance, unlock; default unlock), `oper-state` (enabled, disabled; default disabled), `alarm-report-control` (allowed, inhibited; default Inhibited), label, AID, started-time. Example: `set ikev2-local-instance-1-3 local-address 1.1.180.132`.

On `ikev2-peer`, `re-key-frequency` is the re-key frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end peer, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800. `re-auth-frequency` is the re-authentication frequency, range 3600..604800 seconds, default 43200. The stated rule: re-key-frequency and re-auth-frequency values must not be multiples of each other, and they must have a difference of a few minutes to ensure a significant interval between re-authentication and re-keying. Ranges and defaults may be context-specific. Related attributes are `re-key-fail-policy` (kill traffic, continue traffic; default continue-traffic) with `re-key-traffic-kill-offset` 0..86400 seconds, default 0, and `re-auth-fail-policy` with `re-auth-traffic-kill-offset` 0..86400 seconds, default 0, which set how long the system waits before killing the encrypted SAs tied to this IKE SA.

On `add ipsec-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number>` you must supply `dh-group`; `integrity-algorithm` is optional. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448. integrity-algorithm values: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. `number` is the proposal number, range 1..max, and the spd entry name is a string of length 1..32. Two show-only attributes are fixed: `protocol-id` is ESP and `esn` (Extended Sequence Number support) is esn. Access mode Operational and Candidate Configuration. Example: `add ipsec-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/dns/1 dh-group dhe-3072 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512-256`.

Yes. `ipsec-sa-re-key-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>` supports three re-key triggers for the IPsec child SA with the far-end peer. `frequency` is time based, number in range 3600..86400 seconds, default 14400. `bytes` re-keys on the amount of bytes transmitted, number in range 1048576..max, default 1073741824. `packets` re-keys on the amount of packets transmitted, either disabled or a number in range 1..9223372036854775808, default disabled. All three are available on add, set and show; the object also supports delete. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. So to re-key on volume, set `bytes` (already active by default at 1 GB) or enable `packets`.

The `action` attribute of `ipsec-spd-entry` indicates the IPsec treatment given to matching IP datagrams and takes protect, bypass or discard, with default protect. Yes, it tunnels by default: `mode` takes tunnel or transport with default tunnel. `priority` is mandatory on add (uint8) and gives precedence among SPD entries. Other attributes: `ipsec-protocol` is ESP, `esn` true/false default true, `anti-replay-window` number 32..1024 default 64 and applies when action = protect, `dynamic-ts` disabled/enabled default disabled, `alarm-report-control` allowed/inhibited default allowed, `description` string 0..128, and show-only `oper-state` enabled/disabled default disabled. Example: `add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect`.

Create an `ipsec-traffic-selector` under the SPD entry and then attach the address and port ranges to it. Syntax: `add ipsec-traffic-selector-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name> [next-layer-protocol <value>]`. `next-layer-protocol` indicates the inner (upper layer) protocol taken from the IPv4 protocol or IPv6 next header field, with values any (value 0), opaque (value 255), or a number in range 0-255; default any. The selector name is a string of length 1..64 matching pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*). Addresses and ports are then added as child objects: `local-subnet` and `remote-subnet` with a prefix, and `local-ports` and `remote-ports` with start and stop. Example: `add ipsec-traffic-selector-ipsec/GX2/Radius/ts1 next-layer-protocol 17`.

Because `start` and `stop` are key components of the local-ports AID, not settable attributes. The object is addressed as `local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>` and only `add`, `show` and `delete` forms exist; there is no `set` for local-ports. To change a range you delete the existing instance and add the new one. `start` takes all, opaque or a port number; `stop` is a port-number with default 0, and 0 is only accepted by the system if the starting port is set to all or opaque. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Examples: `add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all` and, for a single port, `add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53`.

Add it under the traffic selector with `add local-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>`. The `prefix` is the key and is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, or broadcast for IPv4 only). Matching `show local-subnet-...` and `delete local-subnet-...` forms exist; there is no set, so to change the subnet you delete and re-add it. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `add local-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/101.10.10.1/32`. The far-end counterpart is `remote-subnet` with the same AID structure.

That is governed by `link-security-control` on the `macsec-entity`, which controls the link security policy for handling data packets when the MACsec connection is not available. Values are must-secure and should-secure, and the default is must-secure, so by default the link must be secured. Set it with `set macsec-entity-<name> link-security-control <value>` (also available on add and show). Other macsec-entity attributes: `enabled` true/false default true, `supporting-facility` (the supporting ethernet facility), `replay-protection` enable/disable, `replay-protection-window` range 0..4294967295 default 0, `alarm-report-control` allowed/inhibited default Inhibited, plus show-only `oper-state` and `negotiated-cipher-suite`. Example: `add macsec-entity-6-3-3 supporting-facility ethernet-6-3-3`.

Use `set macsec-mka-<name> connectivity-association-key <value> connectivity-association-key-name <value>`. Both are strings of length 0..64; the CAK is the pre-shared Connectivity Association Key and the CKN its name. The same command sets `mka-policy` (the mka policy name to use), `psk-lifetime`/`psk-expiration-warning` (range 1..173 days, default 14 days) and `psk-lifetime-enable` (enabled, disabled), plus label and alarm-report-control (allowed, inhibited; default Inhibited). To see which end is the key server, use `show macsec-mka-<name> is-key-server`: it identifies whether the local end is key server, values true/false, default false. `psk-configured-timestamp` shows when the PSK was configured. Example: `set macsec-mka-6-3-3 connectivity-association-key 1122334411223344556677889900112233445566778899001122334455667788 connectivity-association-key-name aa`.

Both live on `mka-policy`, the MACsec Key Agreement policy referenced by the macsec entity related to an ethernet facility. Syntax: `add mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority <value>] [macsec-cipher-suite <value>] [confidentiality-offset <value>] [sak-rekey-interval <value>]`, with matching set, show and `delete mka-policy-<name>`. `macsec-cipher-suite` selects the cipher suites for Secure Association Key (SAK) derivation. `sak-rekey-interval` is the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range '0|30..65535', default 30s. `key-server-priority` is the priority used by the MKA protocol to select the key server. `confidentiality-offset` specifies a number of octets in an Ethernet frame that are sent unencrypted as plain text. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the `re-auth` command, which performs a re-authentication operation of IKEv2 security associations. Syntax: `re-auth [ikev2-peer=]<value>`, where `ikev2-peer` is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), a string with no default. It is an Operational mode command only. Examples: `re-auth ikev2-peer=ikev2-NE202` and `re-auth ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX2`. The scheduled equivalent is the `re-auth-frequency` attribute on the ikev2-peer, range 3600..604800 seconds, default 43200.

The `re-key` command performs a re-key operation, including on-demand re-keying of a data path encryption secure entity, an IKEv2 peer, or an IPsec Child security association (Security Policy Database entry). Syntax: `re-key [ipsec-security-association=]<value> | [ikev2-peer=]<value> | [secure-entity=]<value>`. `ipsec-security-association` points to the IPsec SPD entry object (Child SA), `ikev2-peer` is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), and `secure-entity` points to the secure entity object (Child SA); all three are strings with no default. Access mode is Operational mode. Examples: `re-key secure-entity=NE202-1-4-L1-1` and `re-key ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX`.

Add a remote-ports instance with the starting port set to the keyword `all` and no stopping port: `add remote-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/all`. `start` accepts all, opaque, or a port number. `stop` is a port-number with default 0; if the stopping port is not set the system assumes the value is 0, and 0 is only accepted if the starting port is set to all or opaque, which is why the `all` form needs no stop value. Only add, show and delete are supported, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Examples: `add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all` and, for a single port, `add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49`.

Use `add remote-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>` under the IPsec traffic selector of the SPD entry. The `prefix` is a key and is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, or broadcast for IPv4 only). Matching `show remote-subnet-...` and `delete remote-subnet-...` forms exist; there is no set command, so to change the far-end network you delete and re-add it. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `add remote-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/102.20.20.2/32`. The near-end counterpart is `local-subnet` with the same AID structure.

Use the sc-rx command, which shows the Receiving Secure Channel attributes for MACsec. Syntax: show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. The name is a string of length 0..64 and index is the Receiving Secure Channel Index (uint8). sci-rx is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. The state attribute is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack and takes two values: in-use, meaning Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use, and not-in-use, meaning no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode; only show is supported.

sc-tx reports the Transmitting Secure Channel attributes and is read-only: only show is defined, there is no add, set or delete. Syntax: show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. name is a string of length 0..64, index is the Transmitting Secure Channel Index (uint8), and sci-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier as a hex-string of length 16. state is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack, with values in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) and not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. Assign the certificate with set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>; active-certificate-id is a string 0..128 and accepts a comma-separated list, e.g. set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY. The id is a string 0..20. show secure-application-<id> returns type (server or client), active-certificate-id, in-use (leafref to ../active-certificate-id), and status (enabled or disabled); show secure-applications lists all. To require a client certificate use verify-client-cert, which controls TLS Mutual Authentication: disabled (default) means no client certificate is requested, required means it is required and validated. Changes take effect for new TLS connections only, with no impact on existing connections.

That is controlled by re-key-fail-policy on the secure-entity. It indicates the NE policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful, and takes continue-traffic (the default) or kill-traffic. With the default, traffic is not dropped. If you set kill-traffic, traffic-kill-offset gives the amount of time the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds with a default of 0. The related re-key-frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end peer ranges 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800. All three are settable on add secure-entity-<name> and set secure-entity-<name>. Example: add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is show-only: the syntax is show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group], and there is no add, set or delete. Every algorithm attribute has a single permitted value equal to its default: encryption-algorithm is aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length is key-length-256, integrity-algorithm is none, and dh-group is ecp-521 (the Diffie-Hellman group advertised to the far-end secure entity peer). The proposal number is likewise fixed at 1, with default 1. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Through the security-policy-database object, keyed by the local IKE instance and the peer. Syntax: add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms. ikev2-local-instance is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance and ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA); both are strings. associated-secure-entity is the list of all SPD entries associated with this far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). Example on 1830 GX G40: add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. The cdp command manages manually configured CRL Distribution Points; each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Use add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>], with set, show cdp-<name>, show cdps and delete cdp-<name>. url is an HTTP URL of the form http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>, e.g. http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. enabled (true/false, default false) turns on automatic download and periodic refresh; enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download, and when disabled no refresh is performed but existing CRLs are unaffected. refresh-interval accepts use-next-update (next refresh time from the CRL next-update field) or a duration such as 2w, 5d 12h, 1h 7m 30s. show reports next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result. Requires System Administrator privilege.

Use cert-gen, available in Operational mode: cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]. certificate-name is a string of length 1..128. Validity is set by days, the number of days the certificate is valid for, and defaults to 365. org-name is a string 1..64, common-name is the IP or host name identifying the server (1..64), and subject is the full certificate subject name (1..1024); when generating a self-signed certificate you must specify either subject or common-name. auto-install (true/false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application without an active certificate. -f forces the command without confirmation. Example: cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true.

Through cert-to-name, a prioritized set of rules mapping an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity. Syntax: add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>], with set, show and delete. map-type is extract (take the identity from a certificate field) or map (explicit username). field applies only when map-type is extract: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn, san-uri. mapped-user-name is required only when map-type is map. criteria defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked. priority ranges 1 to 255. issuer filters certificates from a specific issuer (value any). enabled is True or False, default True. Example: add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name.

Use the certificate command in Operational mode. To remove one: clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>, where type is trusted, local or peer, and id is the certificate ID, a string of length 0..128 that must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type (press <tab> to list clearable certificate-ids). -f forces without confirmation; otherwise the CLI prompts Are you sure? [y/n]. Examples: clear certificate local certX, clear certificate type=trusted id=certY. To list what is installed, run show certificates, which displays all managed local/trusted/peer X509v3 certificates imported by the download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; show certificate-revocation shows certificate revocations. The type field also accepts bulk purge options: purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused.

Use clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>. clear-target selects what goes: single-crl (default) removes only the CRL named in <crl-name>, which is then mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL; purge-invalid-crls purges all invalid CRLs; purge-cached-crls purges all CRLs automatically cached from a configured CDP or certificate CDP extension; purge-all-crls purges every CRL. For stale entries only, use purge-invalid-crls, which leaves valid CRLs in place. Examples: clear crl single-crl myCA-1, clear crl purge-invalid-crls. Use <tab> on crl-name to list clearable CRLs. show crls lists installed CRLs and show crl-<name> reports status (valid, expired, future), type (cached or manually), next-update, associated-cdp and downloaded-from-uri. clear is Operational mode; show also works in Candidate Configuration mode.

csr-gen creates a local-certificate in the pending-import state and outputs a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then signed by an external Certificate Authority and the resulting full certificate is downloaded back into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. Until that import happens the local-certificate status shows pending-import (certificate generated by CSR, import not yet complete). Syntax: csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [metadata-from-certificate=]<value> [metadata-from-cnf=]<value> [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] [[key-usage=]<value>] [[extended-key-usage=]<value>]. key-algorithm defaults to eccp256; the subject must include the CN RDN. Access mode is Operational mode. Example: csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia'.

Use display-cert with the display-type parameter: display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>. display-type takes all-certificate-hierarchy (the default), certificate-hierarchy, or certificate-details. Choose certificate-hierarchy to see the trust chain of the specified certificate rather than certificate-details, which prints only that certificate's own contents; all-certificate-hierarchy, the default, shows the hierarchy for all certificates. The certificate parameter is a string naming the certificate to display, and tab completion lists the available names such as local-certificate-pace_client, local-certificate-server_cert and trusted-certificate-ca_root. The command shows the details of a certificate or CSR and runs in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: display-cert trusted-certificate-ca_root.

Use the est command, the Enrollment over Secure Transport client. EST handles certificate requests, renewals and management securely over HTTPS and replaces the manual CSR process. Syntax: est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] [[key-usage=]<value>] [[extended-key-usage=]<value>] [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]. target-command is cacerts, enroll, or re-enroll. est-ca defaults to 1. key-algorithm accepts eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096; signature-hash-algorithm is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256; metadata-template defaults to generic. Example: est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>.

Yes, via auto-re-enrollment on est-ca: set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>]. auto-re-enrollment sets when re-enrollment runs for all leaf certificates issued by that EST CA: a number of days before expiration (1 to 365), or a percentage of the not-after minus not-before interval rounded up, accepted 10% to 90% in 10% increments, or disabled. The default is disabled, so automatic re-enrollment is off until configured. If auto re-enrollment fails the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and it is retried once per day until successful or the certificate becomes invalid. The CA is pinned by explicit-ca-root, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, and root-fingerprint, a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash verifying the Root CA identity. Example: set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40.

The EST server port is set by server-port on the est-server object and defaults to 443. Syntax: add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>], with matching set, delete and show forms. Yes, you can define more than one: priority defines the server's precedence and ranges 1 to 10. If priority is omitted it defaults to the current lowest precedence (highest existing number) plus one; if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. enabled is True or False, default True. path-segment is an optional label added to the EST base url, a string of length 0..64. Example: add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format into the NE from Operational mode. Syntax: import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]; import-certificate -h shows help. The certificate type is local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate. certificate-name is the name the certificate will be known by in the system. passphrase decodes encrypted input certificates for trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. The -i flag imports any intermediate certificates in a PEM bundle; for a single certificate it imports intermediates specified through the AIA extension. Root certificates must be installed individually. Without certificate-name, the name derives from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, e.g. trusted-certificate-Nokia-1. Example: import-certificate peer-certificate certificate-name=peer-cert1 <string in PEM format>.

Check the is-key-in-use attribute on the ISK object: it indicates if the key is in use in this FRU, values true/false, default false. Read it with show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time], or list all with show ISKs. Two related flags: is-key-verified indicates if the key is verified in this FRU (true/false, default false), and being-deleted is true once the system has received an ISK delete command, meaning deletion is already in progress. Remove a key with clear [-f] isk key-name=<value>, giving the name of the key to be deleted; -f forces without confirmation. show works in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode; clear is Operational only.

Use the KRK commands. show KRKs lists the Image Root Keys on the node, and show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] displays one key. name is the unique representation of the object; CPU is the identifier for member CPUs on cards and starts at 0 (uint8); key-name is a string of length 0..64; key-serial-number is a string; issuer-name is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a string of length 0..20; key-length is the key length in bits (uint16); and key-payload is the key payload in hex format, a string of length 0..1100. These commands are show only, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1.

The key-replacement-package command shows key replacement package (KRP) attributes. Syntax: show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]. KRP-version is the package version; issuer-name is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), string 0..20; KRK-name is the KRK (Image root key) that signed this ISK. signature-hash-scheme is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; signature-algorithm is ECDSA, RSA or none; signature-payload is a hex string 0..1024; signature-gen-time is YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. install-status indicates whether the KRP has been installed: not-installed, installing, installed or failed. Show only, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with revocation-mode on local-certificate: set local-certificate-<id> [revocation-mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]. revocation-mode controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined and takes auto (default), force-revoked, or force-unrevoked; force-revoked makes the node treat the certificate as revoked. The id is a string 1..128. Check it with show local-certificate-<id>, whose status reports revoked, expired, untrusted, future, pending-import or valid, and whose used-by attribute lists the secure-applications, ikev2-peers and others presently using the certificate. peer-certificate carries the same revocation-mode attribute with the same values and default. Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>], with set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>], delete ocsp-server-<name>, show ocsp-server and show ocsp-server-<name> [url] [enabled] [priority] [last-query]. name is a string 0..64. url is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder, format http://<host>[:<port>], where host may be an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and port is optional, otherwise default HTTP port 80 is used; string length 0..1024. priority is a uint8 in range 1..10 and sorts the responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, so give the one to try first the lowest number. enabled controls whether the server is consulted for revocation status, true/false, default false. Example: add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application. Manage it with set peer-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>] and show peer-certificate[-id] [version] [serial-number] [subject-name] [issuer] [trust-chain] [valid-from] [valid-to] [status] [white-listed] and more. white-listed is true/false, default false: if true the peer-certificate has no associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain, a leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id. Settable attributes are revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked; default auto), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and label (0..256). The id is 1..128 characters.

The ssh object controls secure shell access; it is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Syntax: set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>] and show ssh [enabled] [port] [pre-login-message] [post-login-message]. The port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell is a number in the range 1..65535 and defaults to 8022. It is not on by default: enabled, which enables direct access to shell via ssh, takes true or false and defaults to false. pre-login-message is the welcome message displayed before user login, a string of length 0..1440 with no default; post-login-message is displayed after login, also 0..1440, and defaults to the standard authorized-users-only warning banner about monitoring. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key entry for that user; each entry holds a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Syntax: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>], plus set (label only), show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label], and delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>. user-name is the user owning the key, local or remote, string 0..32; key-id is a unique identifier for the entry, string 1..64. public-key is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component in PEM format, <key type><SPACE>base64 encoded key<SPACE><comment>, up to 2048 characters. public-key-algorithm is show-only: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096. Example: add ssh-authorized-key-admin/1 public-key AAAAE2VjZHNhLXNoYTIt...

The node's global SSHv2 host keys (used by both server-side and client-side SSHv2 apps) are shown with 'show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm> [public-key] [label] [fingerprint-algorithm] [fingerprint]'. There must be one host key per supported algorithm, so yes, more than one exists. The system auto-generates a host-key in the default DB, and additional host-keys can be added or overwritten via the ssh-keygen RPC. public-key-algorithm values: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096, ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 support starts at R9.0). public-key is PEM/OpenSSH format, String 0..2048 characters; label String 0..256; fingerprint-algorithm md5 or sha256; fingerprint String 0..95 characters. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration. Example: 'show ssh-host-key-ecdsa-sha2-nistp521'.

'ssh-keygen [-b=<key-length>] [-l=<key-label>] [-t=<type>]' generates a private/public key pair and the existing keys in the system are replaced with the newly generated pair. Access mode is Operational mode only. -t selects rsa, ecdsa or ed25519, defaulting to rsa. -b selects strength: RSA 2048, 3072 or 4096 (default 2048); ECDSA 256, 384 or 521 (default 256); ED25519 only 256. If secure mode (security-policies/secure-mode) is enabled, RSA supports only 4096 bits and ECDSA supports only 384 or 521 (default 384); ED25519 stays at 256 irrespective of secure mode. -l sets the key label; if no value is provided the label becomes the value of ne-id. Retrieve the resulting public key with 'show ssh-host-key'.

Create an SSHv2 known hosts entry: 'add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label <value>]'. id is a unique name, String 0..64 characters. address is the hostname, IPv4 or IPv6 address of the allowed/known peer host, optionally with a zone index after a % sign (the device default zone is used if absent). public-key-algorithm is one of ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096, ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 from R9.0). public-key is the OpenSSH Portable host public key in PEM format, String 0..2048 characters. label is String 0..256. 'set ssh-known-host-<id>' can change only the label; also 'show ssh-known-host-<id>' and 'delete ssh-known-host-<id>'. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The trusted-certificate object holds the X509v3 CA (Root and Intermediate) certificates trusted by the system. Syntax: 'set trusted-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]' and 'show trusted-certificate[-id] [version] [serial-number] [subject-name] [issuer] [trust-chain] [valid-from] [valid-to] [status] [public-key-length] [public-key-type] [signature-key-type] [signature-hash-algorithm] [certificate-bytes] [alarm-report-control] [label] [key-usage] [extended-key-usage] [revocation-mode]'. revocation-mode is auto (default), force-revoked or force-unrevoked; alarm-report-control is allowed (default) or inhibited; label 0..256. version is v3; public-key-length rsa2048/rsa3072/rsa4096/ecdsa256/ecdsa384/ecdsa521. Removal is done with the 'clear certificate' command. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'terminate cable-id', which terminates all running CableID verification tests. The terminate command runs in Operational mode ('show cable-id' is also available in Candidate Configuration mode). Because verification is performed on a port-pair basis, the test can be stopped only after the current port-pair verification completes and before the next port-pair starts: the in-progress port-pair runs to completion, then the test exits. The maximum delay to terminate is therefore one port-pair verification time. The test is known to be terminated once cable-id-status cable-id-state changes to idle, so after issuing the command use 'show cable-id cable-id-status' to confirm the entity is back in the idle state.

The CableID signal can only be sourced or terminated by the CAD10A and RD20TM cards; the signal is transparently passed in the OPSM. A CableID path starts at the end A port and terminates at the end Z port, where the signal is sourced/terminated, that is at a CAD10A DWDM port or an RD20TM ADE port. In 'show cable-id-path-<name>', card-type-a and card-type-z take the values RD20TM or CAD10A and identify the CableID capable sled at each end; the value is derived from the provisioned fiber-connection at the port-A/port-Z attribute (when a fiber-connection is created, the CableID function checks whether it is associated with a port on a CableID capable sled and captures the card type into the CableID path topology). port-a and port-z are port AIDs on those sleds.

Yes. cable-id-status is the container holding the process status and progress of a CableID-based fiber connection verification, and you are allowed to issue 'show cable-id cable-id-status' at any time to query the progress. Syntax: 'show cable-id-status [cable-id-state] [test-progress]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. cable-id-state is idle (verification not running, the default), running-incl-switching (running for both active and protected paths) or running-no-switching (running only for the active path). test-progress is a string 0..255 characters, default 'None', reported as 'N out of M completed' where M is the total number of port-pairs to be tested and N the number completed, or 'Not applicable' if cable-id-state is disabled.

Each carrier can discover up to one node. It is possible for multiple collocated carriers to discover the same node multiple times, each time connected to a different remote carrier. View them with 'show carrier-neighbor-<local-carrier> [last-update] [age] [local-carrier-id] [ne-id] [ne-name] [ne-type] [remote-carrier-id] [ipv4-loopback-address] [ipv6-loopback-address]', in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. local-carrier is a string 0..16; ne-id and ne-name strings 0..256; ne-type string 0..64; remote-carrier-id string 0..64, the AID of the remote carrier connected to the local carrier, implying a specific remote port id. last-update is date-time in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. The loopback addresses may be empty if not configured.

Use 'show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. degree-number is uint16 in the range 1..20; it should be greater than zero and not greater than max-degrees. index is uint32 in the range 1..2 but is always 1 in the 1830 GX, since dwdm-line ports are bi-directional. port-name is an instance-identifier giving the dwdm-line port of the RD or ILAx card; as a consequence the OMS of the corresponding dwdm-port is created. Use 'show connection-ports*' to list all connection ports in the node, or for example 'show connection-ports-5/1' to see a single one (output such as port-name port-4-1-dwdm-line1).

Use the custom-tlv command, which shows the list of Organizational Specific TLV (Type-Length-Value) parameter information: 'show custom-tlv-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<oui>/<subtype> [value]'. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. lldp-port is the local port associated with the LLDP agent, string 0..64 characters. direction is ingress or egress. oui is the Organization Unique Identifier of the TLV, the hexadecimal representation of the 24-bit identifier, string 1..6 characters. subtype is the sub-type identifier of the TLV within the scope of that OUI, string 1..507 characters. The value attribute carries the TLV contents.

No. The external-fiber-connection is set autonomously by TNMS; although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. The object is the physical link representation of a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations. Before R8.0, when provisioning one manually the user was also expected to set the port external-connectivity to yes. From R8.0, with l0-mode-op set to slte, external fiber connections can represent intra-NE fibre between RD20TM ADE ports or between CAD10A DWDM and RD20TM ADE ports; for those, scope must be set to cable-id (scope values general-purpose, default, and cable-id). After upgrading to R8.0.1 or later, scope defaults to general-purpose, so existing entries must be deleted and re-added with scope cable-id to enable CableID.

A fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two distinct ports (or two distinct sub-ports) in the same NE, in an OADM/ILA topology. An external-fiber-connection represents a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations, and it is set autonomously by TNMS (manual configuration is possible but not recommended). fiber-connection takes name (0..64), label (0..256), src-port and dst-port instance identifiers, and fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way, default two-way; both add/set/show/delete run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode with no pre- or post-conditions. external-fiber-connection additionally carries scope (general-purpose default, or cable-id), src-node-id/dst-node-id, src-card-name/dst-card-name and src-port-name/dst-port-name.

Yes. icdp is the Nokia Carrier Discovery Protocol, and its global-switch flag defaults to true, so the protocol is enabled by default. Configure it with 'set icdp global-switch <true|false>' and read it back with 'show icdp [global-switch]', both available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: 'set icdp global-switch true'. The icdp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

INCI is the Inter-NE Communication Interface, an API-based communication infrastructure for control plane communication across different network elements, for example between a transponder such as CHM6 on 1830 GX G40 and a line system such as FLEXILS. It uses gRPC server/client as the core mechanism: when the INCI service is enabled the gRPC server is started and bound to the local IP address, and when an INCI neighbor instance is configured gRPC client sessions are established. It is not running by default: the inci-enabled switch takes true or false with a default of false. Use 'set inci [inci-enabled <true|false>]' and 'show inci [inci-enabled]' in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode; for example 'set inci inci-enabled true'.

Compare the configured-node-name you provisioned against the discovered-node-name reported by the far end: 'show inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> [neighbor-address] [neighbor-port] [connection-status] [configured-node-name] [discovered-node-name] [discovered-node-id] [alarm-report-control] [oper-state]'. configured-node-name is the user provisioned name of the remote NE and is explicitly used to compare against the discovered-node-name, which is the name of the remote NE as sent by that NE (both strings 0..128). discovered-node-id is the node ID received from the remote node, string 0..12. oper-state shows enabled or disabled. The neighbor is created with 'add inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> neighbor-address <value> configured-node-name <value> [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>]'; alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited.

Both timers are attributes of interface-neighbor: 'set interface-neighbor-<local-interface> [discovery-cycle-time <value>] [discovery-timeout <value>] [discovery-enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]'. discovery-cycle-time is the periodicity at which sndp discover messages are sent, range 30..300 seconds, default 30. discovery-timeout is the time after which discovery is considered failed, range 300..1800 seconds, default 300; when the timeout occurs neighbor-adjacency-state transitions to blackout. discovery-enabled is true or false, default true. neighbor-adjacency-state values are blackout, discovery, holding and unknown (default unknown). oper-state is enabled or disabled, default disabled; alarm-report-control allowed (default) or inhibited. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. 'show links' displays the links container within the topology, and these links are dynamically filled in by the system, allowing the NCT topology to be derived and displayed. The command takes no parameters and is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The related nct-connection command shows the individual NCT port-to-port links in a multi-chassis NE, and those links are likewise dynamically filled in by the system.

The retention period is the global LLDP hold-on-timer, set with 'set lldp [hold-on-timer <value>]' and read with 'show lldp [hold-on-timer]', in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. hold-on-timer is a number of seconds and defaults to 900. It is the time to keep neighbor information in the case where the neighbor does not supply an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) TLV. Where a remote system does provide a TTL, the per-neighbor ttl attribute in 'show lldp-neighbor' gives the number of seconds until that information expires; if the remote system does not provide a ttl value, that parameter is set to the global hold-on-timer. Example: 'set lldp hold-on-timer 60'. The lldp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

'show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> [chassis-id-subtype] [chassis-id] [port-id-subtype] [port-id] [port-description] [system-name] [system-description] [supported-capabilities] [enabled-capabilities]' shows the LLDP local system information sent on an LLDP port. On the 1830 GX: chassis-id-subtype is chassis-component and chassis-id is the chassis serial number; port-id-subtype is local and port-id is the port AID; port-description is the port name; system-name is the NE name; and system-description is the string 'Nokia Corporation.Converged OS, Version <release id> _ build <software label>'. All these strings are 0..255 characters. supported-capabilities and enabled-capabilities are router and bridge. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: 'show lldp-local-info-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4'.

No, the egress direction is not supported. In 'show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/<direction> [last-update] [age] [chassis-id-subtype] [chassis-id] [port-id-subtype] [port-id] [port-description] [system-name] [system-description] [supported-capabilities] [enabled-capabilities] [ttl]', the only direction value is ingress, so use for example 'show -r lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-1-3/ingress'. The same restriction applies to lldp-port-statistics. The discovered remote system information is kept indefinitely until the port is decommissioned or the data is manually cleared by the user. age is the number of seconds since discovery and ttl is the number of seconds until the remote information expires, falling back to the global hold-on-timer if the remote system supplies no ttl. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. All counter values in a particular lldp-port-statistics entry are maintained on a continuing basis and are not deleted upon expiration of the TTL timing counters associated with the LLDP neighbor information. The counters do freeze: all statistical counters associated with a particular port on the local LLDP agent become frozen whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled for that port. Syntax: 'show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/<direction> [last-change-time] [last-clear-time] [total-ageouts] [total-discarded-frames] [error-frames] [total-frames-in] [total-frames-out] [total-discarded-tlvs] [total-unrecognized-tlvs]'; direction is ingress only, egress is not supported. Counters default to 0; total-ageout counts the times a neighbor's information was deleted from the lldp-neighbor list due to TTL expiry. last-clear-time defaults to 0000-01-01T00:00:00Z.

Use 'show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> [src-chassis] [dst-chassis] [src-chassis-state] [dst-chassis-state]', which shows NCT connectivity information, the existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE; the links are dynamically filled in by the system so the NCT topology can be derived. src-chassis-state and dst-chassis-state take the values node controller, provisioned and unprovisioned. src-port and dst-port must be NCT ports: for a commissioned chassis the port AID is used, for an unprovisioned chassis the format is '<chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>'. Likewise src-chassis and dst-chassis show the chassis AID when commissioned and the chassis serial number when unprovisioned; all four are strings 0..64. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The sndp command controls the SNDP feature through a single switch: 'set sndp [sndp-enabled <value>]' and 'show sndp [sndp-enabled]', both available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. sndp-enabled takes true or false and defaults to true, so the feature is on by default. Example: 'show sndp sndp-enabled'. SNDP discover messages are the ones sent on a management interface at the periodicity given by the interface-neighbor discovery-cycle-time attribute (range 30..300 seconds, default 30).

'add submarine-link-<name> src-node-id <value> src-port-name <value> dst-node-id <value> dst-port-name <value> degree-target-tx-power <value> ...' The mandatory attributes are src-node-id and dst-node-id (the NE names of the source and destination nodes, strings 0..256), src-port-name and dst-port-name (the OTS dwdm-line port of the degree at each endpoint, strings 0..128) and degree-target-tx-power, the launch power at the ROADM into the primary fiber. fiber-length is the fibre length in km of the associated fiber pair, decimal64 in the range 0..25000 km with a default of 0, excluding branch segment lengths. Other attributes: fiber-connection-type two-way (default) or one-way, link-name, fiber-pair-id, segment-list, bu-segment-index (uint16, default 0), rx/tx-fiber-type, gsnr, degree-expected-rx-power, commissioning-snr-margin, launch-condition flat-tx or pfib (default pfib), and allocated-spectrum-list, max 32 elements.

'show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> [fiber-connection-list]' shows the list of fiber connections supporting an entity. name is the entity name, a String 0..64 characters, and fiber-connection-list is an instance-identifier giving the supported fiber connection path. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The same container appears under cable-id-path when the -r flag is used: 'show -r cable-id-path-<name>' displays, for a single port, the results from the port-pair including all cable-id-path parameters plus the supporting-fiber-connection container and its fiber-connection-list, for example 'fiber-connection-list supporting-fiber-connection-R1'.

Use clear topology to remove stale neighbour data: clear [-f] topology [target=]<value>. The target is an instance-identifier and may be an lldp-neighbor instance (discovered via LLDP), a carrier-neighbor instance (discovered via ICMP), or an lldp-port-statistics instance (details associated with an LLDP enabled port). Tip: type clear topology <tab> to get the list of valid topology objects. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: clear topology lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-4-T1-1. Access Mode is Operational Mode, with Candidate Configuration Mode allowed only for the show command. show topology retrieves topology information and accepts inci, links, lldp, icdp or sndp.

Trigger it with verify [-f] [type-select=]<value> [[target-select=]<value>] [allow-switching]. type-select currently supports only fiber-connection. target-select is the port instance-identifier of the CableID-capable card; if the port-id is not specified the verification is done on all paths, and if the port is in multiple CableID paths all of them are checked. allow-switching is boolean, default false: false verifies active paths only (no system initiated switching, so an in-service system is not disturbed), true lets CableID initiate switching on the OPSM so both active and inactive paths are verified. Pre-condition: equipment-policies cable-id-control must be set to enabled. The command prompts for confirmation unless -f is used, raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE, and is non-blocking; poll with show cable-id-status. Example: verify fiber-connection port-1-6-ade3 allow-switching=true.

The bert command runs in Operational Mode. Start: bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=ingress test-duration=10. test-signal-type takes none (default), PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV or scrambled-idles; 100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles and ODU4 uses PRBS31/PRBS31NONINV. test-signal-monitoring-type adds fec-frames for CarrierCTP. Directions are ingress or egress. test-duration is in seconds with min 10 and max up to 1000 hrs; the default 0 means indefinite. If no test-id is given the system generates one. Stop or abort with bert stop test-id=TestX; test-id is mandatory for stop. Also bert get and bert delete, by test-id or by resource. Multiple simultaneous BERTs can run on a facility if each fulfils the pre-conditions.

You cannot create it; the cid-ptp facility is created by the system when a card supporting the CableID function is created, for example RD20TM or CAD10A. It represents the CableID SFP and its connection to the card via the CID port. managed-by therefore reads system, and only user-created facilities can be user deleted. Only set and show are offered: set cid-ptp-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <value>] and show cid-ptp-<name> with supporting-card, supporting-port, AID, oper-state, avail-state, managed-by and used. admin-state is not editable and the only supported value is unlock; CableID operation is not affected by the cid-ptp admin-state. used is true when CableID functionality is supported (default false). Example: show cid-ptp-1-4-spcid.

The eth-zr Digital Coherent 400ZR facility is auto-instantiated when the ZR TOM is provisioned; interface-type reports 400ZR (Media-interface 400ZR-CFEC-DP-16QAM) and rate is 400.000 Gbit/s. fec-type defaults to ofec and accepts not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4 (EFEC-I4), i7 (EFEC-I7), sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 and ufec7. Degrade monitoring is off by default: fdd-monitoring and fed-monitoring are enabled/disabled with default disabled. The four thresholds are decimal64(9) in average BER, range 0.000000001..0.1: fdd-threshold default 0.0195, fdd-clear-threshold 0.01062, fed-threshold 0.0206, fed-clear-threshold 0.01125. Set with, for example, set eth-zr-1-6-T8 fed-threshold 0.011870000. link-degrade-indication shows none, local-degraded, remote-degraded or local-and-remote-degraded.

max-packet-length on the ethernet facility is the maximum transfer unit in octets. The default is 1518. The range is 1280..18000 octets on the 1830 GX G30 and 1518..18000 octets on the 1830 GX G40. Configure with set ethernet-<name> max-packet-length <value> and read it with show ethernet-<name> max-packet-length. Two stated restrictions apply: the parameter is configurable on card level only and applies to all interfaces in that card, and it is used only for determining the undersized/oversized packet count in 100GbE PMs. Access Mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

show facilities lists the facilities configured on the node. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The output is a flat list of facility instance names; on a 1830 GX G40 it includes entries such as super-channel-group-1-4-L1, super-channel-1-4-L1-1, optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1, optical-channel-1-4-L1-1, trib-ptp-1-4-T11, comm-channel-1-4-L1-1, otu-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni, otu-1-4-T11, ethernet-1-4-T2, odu-1-4-L1-1-ODUCni and odu-1-4-L2-1-ODUflexi-1. To read attributes of any listed entry, use that facility's own command, for example show ethernet-1-4-T2.

The fc command (set fc-<name> / show fc-<name>) covers Fibre Channel. fc-type is read-only and reports FC1G, FC2G, FC4G, FC8G, FC16G or FC32G.
