Two settings are FC specific: tts enables or disables Transmitter Training Signal support for the 32GFC client (enabled or disabled, default disabled), and laser-toggling-for-tts enables or disables laser toggling when tts is enabled/disabled for the 32GFC client (enabled or disabled, default enabled). The remainder are common facility attributes: label, admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode (GMP default, also BMP, openZR+, FlexE-4x100G, GFP-F, GFP-F-extOPU2, AMP, iGMP, none), loopback (none/facility/terminal), loopback-mode, test-signal-type (default none), test-signal-direction (default ingress) and test-signal-monitoring (default false).

foic-type on the flexo facility is show-only. FOICx.k means k parallel lanes carrying a FlexO-x interface, where order x is the interface rate in units of 100G (a unique FOICx.k identification per G.709.3 FlexO-LR and G.709.1 FlexO-SR). Supported values are foic1.2, foic1.4, foic2.4, foic2.8, foic3.6, foic4.8 and foic4.16, with foic4.8 the default. resource-mode is settable and selects the resource mode to support ADM (add-drop) or XC (add-drop with regen); the default is ADM. Change it with set flexo-1-5-L1-1 resource-mode 'XC'. fec-type is show-only with values not-applicable, cfec, ofec and noFEC, default ofec. Other settable attributes are label, admin-state, alarm-report-control, iid and the fdd/fed raise and clear thresholds.

add flexo-group-<name> requires four mandatory attributes: carriers, rate, modulation-format and group-id. carriers is the list of carriers bound to this facility, string length 1..32. rate is the carried signal basic rate class in Gbit/s. modulation-format is one of not-applicable, DP-QPSK, DP-16QAM, DP-8QAM or BPSK. group-id indicates the interface group instance that the FlexO-x interface is a member of and must be unique in the NE; it is an integer in range 1..1048575. Optional on add are label (0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed) and fec-type (default ofec). Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode; remove with delete flexo-group-<name>.

high-speed-monitoring is a node-level object with exactly two attributes, both settable and viewable: set high-speed-monitoring [enabled <value>] [port <value>] and show high-speed-monitoring [enabled] [port]. enabled is the user configurable switch to enable or disable high speed monitoring; values true or false, default false. port is the user configurable port, uint16 in range 1..max, default 57500. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The interlaken facility represents the SPN2 Interlaken interface. capacity is the total capacity for the interlaken interface and is show-only, fixed at 500 Gbit/s. Only four attributes are settable with set interlaken-<name>: label (string 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and loopback (none, facility for a test towards the facility side, or terminal for a test towards the terminal side; default none). Everything else is show-only, including supporting-card, supporting-port, supporting-facilities, supported-facilities, AID, oper-state, avail-state, managed-by (system) and capacity. Example: set interlaken-66-1-8 label interlaken_66_1.

On line-ptp, auto-in-service is switched by auto-in-service-enabled, true or false with default false, available on add, set and show. The facility is automatically enabled once a valid signal has been detected for valid-signal-time, the configurable time that represents detection of a valid signal, in the range 1..7200 minutes with default 480. remaining-valid-signal-time is show-only (1..7200 minutes) and reports the actual remaining time for the facility to be automatically enabled by the auto-in-service mechanism; a typical show gives valid-signal-time 480 minutes and remaining-valid-signal-time 0 minutes. Configure with set line-ptp-<name> auto-in-service-enabled true valid-signal-time <minutes>. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

They are two separate commands. show network-xconnect is read-only: it shows the list of services of multiple user cross connections commissioned in this NE, takes no parameters, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. nw-xconnect is the provisioning object, with add, delete, set and show: add nw-xconnect-<name> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [xcon-type <value>] [rate <value>], set nw-xconnect-<name> [rate <value>], show nw-xconnect-<name> [AID] [oper-state] [avail-state] [endpoint1] [endpoint2] [xcon-type] [rate], and delete nw-xconnect-<name>. xcon-type is L1-ETH-TO-GCC0, L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0, L1-ETH-TO-OSC or L1-OSC-TO-OSC (default L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0), and rate is 1..20 Mbps. Use network-xconnect to inspect, nw-xconnect to create.

nw-xconnect provides four user channel cross-connection types and there is no direct GCC0-to-OSC type: xcon-type is L1-ETH-TO-GCC0, L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0, L1-ETH-TO-OSC or L1-OSC-TO-OSC, default L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0. endpoint1 and endpoint2 are mandatory at creation. For L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 and L1-ETH-TO-OSC, endpoint1 is an instance-identifier to a comm-eth MO of a chassis; for L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0 it is a GCC0 comm-channel MO; for L1-OSC-TO-OSC it is an OSCX-5 comm-channel MO. endpoint2 is a GCC0 comm-channel for the GCC0 types and an OSC-5 comm-channel for the OSC types. rate is uint8 1..20 Mbps, default 13 for L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 and 20 for L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC. Example: add nw-xconnect-test1 xcon-type L1-ETH-TO-OSC endpoint1 comm-eth-1-16-ETH4 endpoint2 comm-channel-1-6-dwdm-line-OSCX5.

No. The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created. When a CHM6 has an OTU configured on it, use show odu to determine whether the ODU already exists. The class attribute is set by the system based on order of creation: high-order marks the top-most ODUCn/ODUk entity created by the system, low-order is the default for children, and mapped indicates a mapped non-OTN or OTN client signal. What you add yourself are the low order ODUs that XCONs map into, ODU4i (100G) or ODUflexi (400G): add odu-<name> odu-type <value> parent-odu <HO-ODU name> time-slots <list>, for example add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu '1-7-L1-1-ODUCni' time-slots 1..80. Pre-condition: the super-channel must be added before low order ODUs can be added.

Yes. odu-diagnostics is keyed per direction: the instance is odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> where direction is ingress or egress, and each direction has its own values. So issue set odu-diagnostics-<name>/ingress tx-tti <value> and set odu-diagnostics-<name>/egress tx-tti <value> separately. tti-style is also per direction: ITU-T-G709 (the default) splits the TTI into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes, while proprietary makes it a single 64 byte string. tx-tti and expected-tti take a hex string with 0x prefix (length 1..130) or printable ASCII (length 1..64); tx-sapi and tx-dapi are 1..15 characters and tx-operator 1..32. monitoring-mode (default intrusive) and tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting (default disabled) are likewise per direction. Example: set odu-diagnostics-Lodu4i/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI-DAPI-OPER.

Yes, FEC is on by default. On the otu facility, fec-mode is the configured Forward Error Correction mode on the OTUk/OTUCn client; values enabled or disabled, default enabled. fec-generation-mode is the configured FEC generation mode towards the far-end receiver; values enabled or disabled, default also enabled. fec-type defaults to ofec, with permitted values not-applicable, cfec, ofec, G709, noFEC, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 and ufec7. All three are available on add, set and show, for example set otu-<name> fec-type cfec. The read-only service-mode-qualifier can report nofec when the OTU is carried without FEC. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting on otu-diagnostics; it indicates whether the TTI-Mismatch (TIM) alarm is reported or masked and, if reported, the criteria used. To alarm only on a mismatched source trace, set it to SAPI: set otu-diagnostics-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI. The values are disabled (default), full-64-bytes, SAPI, DAPI, OPER, SAPI-DAPI, SAPI-OPER, DAPI-OPER and SAPI-DAPI-OPER. The attribute is per direction; the instance is otu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> with direction ingress or egress. Pair it with expected-sapi (hex with 0x prefix length 1..32, or printable ASCII 1..15) and tti-style ITU-T-G709, the default, which splits the TTI into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes. tim-act-enabled (default disabled) decides whether a maintenance signal is inserted on TIM.

The stm facility terminates STM-16 and STM-64 only: stm-type, the type of SDH signal (STM-N), is show-only with values STM-16 and STM-64. The name is the Synchronous Transport Module N, for example N=16 or 64, per reference ITU-T G.691. Configurable attributes via set stm-<name> include label, admin-state (Lock, Unlock, Maintenance; default Unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode, tti-style (ITU-T-G709 default, or proprietary), tim-monitor (enabled or disabled, default disabled), tx-tti and expected-tti (tti-64), loopback-mode (none, facility, terminal; default none), test-signal-type (none, PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31; default none) and test-signal-monitoring. Example: set stm-1-5-T9.2 tx-mapping-mode BMP.

That is trib-ptp tributary-disable-action: it indicates what the network element performs towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting an appropriate replacement signal. Values are laser-shut-off (the default), none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (1830 GX G30 only). tributary-disable-holdoff-timer is the hold off time of client shutdown or replacement signal at egress, uint16 range 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 meaning holdoff disabled; it applies only when the TDA action is Laser-turnoff. Related switches are near-end-tda (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (default disabled) and forward-defect-trigger (true/false, default true). Example: set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off.

Create it with add xcon-<name> source <value> destination <value> [payload-type <value>] [direction <value>] [label <value>] [circuit-id-suffix <value>], where source and destination are the end-point Instance IDs. direction supports only two-way, which is the default. Example: add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1, or on a G30 add xcon-11 source odu-1-1-3-ODU4 destination odu-1-1-1-ODU4-1. After creation only label and circuit-id-suffix can be changed with set. protection-type is show-only and reports the protection type this XCON has: y-cable, snc-n, snc-i or unprotected, with unprotected the default. Other show-only attributes are type (add, drop, add-drop, express), payload-treatment, network-mapping and managed-by (default user; only user created XCONs can be user deleted).

An L2-bridge is identified by bridge-name, the name of the bridge, a string of length 0..64 that forms the instance name L2-bridge-<bridge-name>. It has just two attributes, both settable and viewable: chassis-name, a leafref to the chassis associated with this L2 bridge, and description, a string of length 0..255 describing the bridge and its intended purpose. Syntax is set L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name <value>] [description <value>] and show L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name] [description]. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Only set and show verbs are documented for this command.

Use clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>. app-name is the third party app name. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. clear is the only verb on the app command, and it clears third party apps. If instead you want to act on a running third-party application rather than remove it, use appctl, which takes app-name plus a command of restart, netls or exec, an optional target (system or a chassis/card AID) and optional parameters.

Use appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[parameters=]<value>[,<value>]*]. app-name is a leafref to the third-party-app app-name under ne/system/sw-management. command is one of restart (restarts the third party application), netls (shows the list of subnet networks used by the containers) or exec (execute the third party application operation given in parameters). target says whether the command is executed for the entire system or for a chassis/card AID; it takes a string or system, default system. parameters is an optional list of strings with max-elements 50, applicable when command is restart or exec. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Use the call-home command in Operational Mode: `call-home [dial-out-server-name=]<string>`. It executes a manual connection trigger to a configured dial-out-server and forces a connection attempt. If a dial-out-server is currently in the 'connecting' state, call-home forces an immediate attempt and will not wait for some time before retrying. Pre-condition: the dial-out server must be configured for this command to execute properly. The dial-out-server-name parameter is the pre-configured name of the dial-out server (string, no default). `call-home -h` displays help. Example: `call-home collector-x`.

Use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name> [related-session-id] [related-dial-out-server] [session-type] [session-protocol] [encoding] [transfer-mode] [updates-only] [user-access]` (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). encoding specifies the data encoding scheme for data sent to and from the target device: json, bytes, proto, ascii, json-ietf, default json-ietf. transfer-mode specifies the data transfer mode: stream (values streamed by the target), once (values sent once-off), poll (values sent in response to a poll request), default stream. session-protocol is gnmi (default gnmi), and session-type is gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel or gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc. updates-only is true/false, default false. subscription-name is a string of length 0...128.

No. The data-model `enabled` attribute defaults to false, so a model is not loaded until you turn it on. Use `set data-model-<name> enabled true` to load it; enabled allows loading/unloading the data model, and a loaded data model means it can be used via the management interfaces. Values are true/false. To inspect models use `show data-model-<name> [description] [enabled]`, or `show data-model` to view all available YANG data models for loading/unloading. name is a String of length 0..256 (used in set and show) and description is a String of length 0..256 (show only). Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The dial-out-server retry-policy is one of progressive-back-off (default), retry-then-stop, or retry-forever. `retry` is the number of retries, Integer range 0..5, default 3, and is only applicable when retry-policy is retry-then-stop. `timeout` is the timeout before the next retry, Integer range 1..255 seconds, default 10, and is not applicable for progressive-back-off, which has a dynamic timeout. The `port` is the dial-out-server session port, Integer range 1..65535, default 4334 (the default for the netconf protocol over ssh). protocol is netconf (default) or restconf; transport is ssh. auto-connect defaults to true; if false the server can still be connected manually via the call-home RPC. Example: `add dial-out-server-callhome1 address 10.220.87.52 port 4337`.

Yes, gRPC/gNMI is enabled by default: the grpc `enabled` attribute is true/false with default true. The `port` which listens for gNMI access via gRPC defaults to 50051. Configure with `set grpc [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity <value>]` and inspect with `show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity]` in Operational or Candidate Configuration Mode. gnmi-get-encoding-granularity controls the granularity of data in gNMI Get responses when encoded with JSON: per-path puts all path data in one Update message, per-object divides the path data into multiple Update messages, one per YANG container/list entry; the default is per-object. The grpc object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

NETCONF listens on the `port` attribute for access via ssh: port-number (uint16, range 1..65535) with default 830. `hello-timeout` specifies the number of seconds that a session may exist before the hello PDU is received/transmitted; a session will be dropped if no hello PDU is received/transmitted before that number of seconds elapses. It is a uint16 in the range 1..3600 seconds with a default of 2. Set them with `set netconf [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [annotate-cli-name <value>] [static-info-in-notifs <value>] [hello-timeout <value>]`. NETCONF `enabled` defaults to true, and it is not possible to disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session. annotate-cli-name defaults to false.

Plain HTTP is available but off by default: `http-enabled` is true/false with default false, and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. `https-enabled` defaults to true. The http-port defaults to 8080 and the https-port to 8181, both Numbers in the range 1..65535, and the overall `enabled` switch defaults to true. Session length is governed by `cookie-timeout`, the timeout of a cookie based RESTCONF session, a Number in the range 1..300 minutes with default 5; the cookie expiration date is reset every time there is activity on the session. Example: `set restconf cookie-timeout 10`. `api-root` (String 0..64) is show-only.

Use `show snmp [enabled] [port] [snmp-engine-id] [engine-boot-count]` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. snmp-engine-id is a show-only String (length 0..256) giving the SNMP EngineID of the NE; it follows the EngineID format 3 defined in RFC3411, and the MAC address in the Engine ID is the first MAC address of the MAC address pool of the NE. engine-boot-count is a show-only Number (uint16, default 0) that counts how many times the engine has restarted. The settable attributes are `enabled` (true/false, default true) for global SNMP access and `port`, the port where the NE listens for SNMP requests, Number range 1..65535, default 161. Note the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object.

No. The snmp-community attribute `community-string-access` is the SNMP access right of the community string and its only permitted value is read-only, which is also the default. Create a community with `add snmp-community-<name> community-string <value> [enabled <value>] [community-string-access <value>]`, and edit or inspect with set/show; `delete snmp-community-<name>` removes it. `name` is the name for the community, different from the community string itself, String length 0..64; `community-string` is a String of length 1..32; `enabled` is false/true with default true. Note the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Example: `add snmp-community-mycommunity community-string public community-string-access read-only enabled true`.

Add a trap listener with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]`. `snmp-version` is v2c or v3, default v2c. `trap-community-string` is the community string used for SNMP traps, String 0...32, default infinera. `target-port` is the UDP port number, Number range 0..65535, default 162, and `target-transport` is udp (default udp). `enabled` defaults to true and target-name is a String 0...32. snmpv3-user is applicable when snmp-version is v3. Example: `add snmp-target-mytarget snmp-version v2c target-ip 10.220.225.10 target-port 162 target-transport udp trap-community-string public enabled true`.

A new SNMPv3 user gets `user-sec-level` no-auth-no-priv by default; the permitted values are auth-no-priv, auth-priv and no-auth-no-priv. The privacy protocol `priv-protocol` can be DES, AES128, AES192 or AES256, with default AES128. `auth-protocol` has only the value SHA (default SHA). Create with `add snmpv3-user-<snmpv3-user-name> auth-passphrase <value> priv-passphrase <value> [user-sec-level <value>] [auth-protocol <value>] [priv-protocol <value>]`; auth-passphrase and priv-passphrase are mandatory Strings of length 8...64 and the user name is a String of length 1...32. Example: `add snmpv3-user-bob user-sec-level auth-priv auth-protocol SHA auth-passphrase public123 priv-protocol AES128 priv-passphrase private123`.

The `subscription-path-mode` attribute states how subscription updates are sent: target-defined (default), on-change, or sample. Inspect it with `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name> [subscription-path] [subscription-path-origin] [subscription-path-mode] [sample-interval] [heartbeat-interval] [suppress-redundant]`. `sample-interval` is the time in milliseconds between samples of the telemetry data source, default 0 (set to 0 when optional); for a target-defined stream subscription, if the sample-interval is not set the system automatically adjusts it from 0 to 10 seconds. `heartbeat-interval` is the maximum interval in milliseconds between updates, default 0; if sample-interval is not set and heartbeat-interval is lower than 10 seconds, the system adjusts it to 20 seconds. `suppress-redundant` is true/false, default true.

`show subscriptions` shows the list of subscriptions. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For more detail on the telemetry subscriptions configured in the system, use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>`, which reports related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type, session-protocol, encoding, transfer-mode, updates-only and user-access. For the paths within a subscription, use `show subscription-path` or `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>`, which reports subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode, sample-interval, heartbeat-interval and suppress-redundant.

Telemetry is configured through the `telemetry` object: `show telemetry` and `set telemetry id <string>`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. This command is used to configure persistent and dynamic telemetry, and the object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Its only parameter is `id`, described as persistent and dynamic telemetry, a string of length 0..4096 with no default. The guide does not define the two terms further. The subscriptions themselves are viewed with `show subscriptions` and `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>`, where session-type distinguishes gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel and gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc sessions.

Use `show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable]`, or per location `show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]`. The `state` attribute is the third party app state, with values running, stopped and failed, and its default is stopped. It is not enabled by default: `enable` is the third-party-app enabled state, true/false with default false. If enabled, the app is started and is also enabled upon system restart; if disabled, the app is stopped. Set with `set third-party-app-<app-name> [state <value>] [enable <value>] ...`. To control a running app use `appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]<value>` with command restart, netls or exec.

The `add` command creates a new managed entity: `add [-v|-m|-f] <entity id> [(<attribute> <value>) ...]`. Use `add <tab>` to visualize all entity types that are creatable at that time, and `add -h` for help. The add command page also lists the creatable entities with a page reference for each one (for example aaa-server, access-rule, ace, acl, card, cdp, chassis, dial-out-server, interface, snmp-community, snmp-target, snmpv3-user, task, template, tom, user, user-group, xcon), and each of those pages gives that entity's attributes. Some entities have mandatory attributes that must be provided on creation; if a mandatory attribute is not provided in the command itself, the CLI automatically asks for it. Entities managed by the system cannot be created with add. -v validates only, -m merges (a best effort add), -f forces without confirmation.

Yes. In all cases the `clear` command requires a user confirmation, and a confirmation prompt is displayed if the -f flag is not provided; -f forces the command without confirmation. Syntax is `clear [-f] <subcommand> ...` and the access mode is Operational Mode; `clear -h` displays help. The subcommands are alarm, app, certificate, crl, database, dns, file, isk, log, ospf, pm, recover-mode, statistics, system and topology, for example `clear -f pm`, `clear -f topology target=<value>` or `clear -f system type=<value>`. Note that `clear system factory-reset` with the `shutdown` option is not supported on the L0 cards.

Yes, with the cli attribute `show-alarm-columns`, which selects the columns to display in the output of the 'show alarm' CLI command. Permitted values are a list of columns separated by a comma, `default-columns` to show the pre-defined columns, or `default-columns,<additional-details>` to add the <additional-details> column to the pre-defined columns. The default is default-columns, and this configuration has a global effect, taking effect on all CLI sessions. Examples: `set cli show-alarm-columns col1,col2,col3` and `set cli show-alarm-columns default-columns,corrective-action`. The same command also carries enabled (default true, cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port (range 1..65535, default 22) and default-interactive-mode (default true).

Use `set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>`. cli-lines is the configurable number of rows to be used for display before pausing the output; after pausing, pressing [SPACEBAR] resumes display. Its range is 10..1000 with a default of 40. The companion attribute cli-columns is the number of columns used for display, range 80..4000, default 80. The same command also sets interactive-mode (true/false, default true; set per CLI session and not persistent) and display-timestamp (true/false, default false). Inspect with `show cli-session-config-<session-id> [cli-lines] [cli-columns] [interactive-mode] [display-timestamp]`. Example: `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-lines 30`.

Yes. The `connect` command establishes an ssh session directly from the CLI: `connect [target-address=]<value> [user-name=]<value> [[port=]<value>]`, access mode Operational Mode. target-address is a mandatory attribute and may be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address or a hostname if DNS is configured; it requires connectivity. user-name is a string of 0..64 characters. port is optional: by default port 22 is used, but it can be provided if needed, which is useful to access the shell port. Example: `connect 10.41.24.55 admin port=8022`, which then prompts for the remote user's password.

Yes, use `convert [target-representation=]<value> [command=]<value>`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The target-representation values are netconf-xml (an entire NETCONF xml payload), netconf-python (Python code performing a NETCONF request), restconf-json (HTTP method, URI, headers and body with JSON payloads), restconf-xml (the same with XML payloads), restconf-python, plaintext-to-encrypted, snmp-oids and netsnmp-cmd. Multiple CLI commands can be given separated by ';' and are merged where possible. The generated Python is compatible with Python 2 and 3 and requires ncclient for NETCONF or requests for RESTCONF; host, IP and user-name are auto filled, only the password must be entered manually. Example: `convert restconf-python 'ping 1.23.151.23'`.

No. The `default` command assigns default values to the targeted entities, but some of the configuration attributes will not be reset to default, including mandatory parameters and attributes only settable at creation. Syntax is `default [-f] [entity-id=][,]* [[attribute=][,]*]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. If attributes are specified, only those are set to their default value; otherwise all possible configuration attributes are defaulted. Multiple instances can be selected using the wildcard (*), for example `default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/*` or `default alarm-severity-entry-*`. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation, and -h displays help. The default command is not supported in 1830 GX G30 Releases 5.0 and 5.1.

Use the -b flag: `delete -b <object>` is the best effort delete introduced in R9.0. Standard behaviour is that `delete <object>` fails if the object does not exist, whereas `delete -b <object>` does not fail if the object does not exist; it only bypasses the check for object existence. It may still produce other errors, such as precondition failures, and it has the same functionality as a NETCONF 'remove' operation. Full syntax is `delete [-f|-v|-b] <entity-id> [<filter> ...]`, where -f forces the command without the confirmation prompt (useful in scripts, since delete otherwise prompts) and -v validates only, replying 'OK' if valid.

`exit` logs out of the current CLI mode: it terminates the current CLI session if you are in operational mode, or leaves configuration mode if you are in candidate mode. A confirmation prompt is displayed unless the -f flag is provided, so `exit -f` exits without confirmation. Syntax is `exit [-h|-f]`, where -h displays help for the command and -f forces the command without confirmation. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl+D has the same effect as `exit -f`.

Use the `expect` command, which ensures that an attribute matches an expected value: `expect [-r] [<instance>=]<value> [<expected-value>=]<value> [<attribute>=]<value>`, as in `expect ne ne-name GX-NE-123`. If the value matches, no output is seen; if it does not, an ERROR message is shown. It is intended for scripts and automation to guarantee specific assumptions and can be invoked multiple times to validate multiple attributes, but wildcards to select multiple object instances or attributes are not supported. If the script is executed in 'stop-on-error' mode, a failed expect stops the script immediately. The -r flag enables regex mode, making the expected-value a regular expression instead of a literal string, for example `expect -r software-load-active swload-version R5.*`.

Yes, with the export command, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Syntax: export [-h] or export [<variable>=[<value>]]. Variables are referenced as ${variable} in any CLI command. The variable name can be any alphanumeric name; the value can be any supported character, including spaces. export SLOT_NUMBER=2 declares one, export SLOT_NUMBER= deletes it, and export with no arguments lists all existing variables, for example: export MYSESSIONID="10.100.152.29:56154" and export MYUSERNAME="admin". Variables are locally defined per session, so they are removed after the session is closed; they do not survive logout. The functionality is particularly useful in CLI scripts.

shell launches a Linux bash shell from within the CLI on the node itself. It runs as the currently logged-in user and allows the commands accessible to that user; access to the shell command can be limited to users in the NA, NE and TT user-groups. Certain commands/scripts can be launched with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo', restricted to a fixed list (/bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and the /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts). gshell launches a bash shell inside a Guest Container instead, and has the pre-condition that the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Both are Operational mode, both accept a single command to execute (shell ifconfig, gshell ls -l), and both return to the CLI prompt when the shell is closed with exit.

No. kill-session <session-id> closes any established session independently of its type (CLI, NETCONF, etc.), but the <session-id> must match an existing session-id in the form '<ip-address>:<port>' and cannot match the id for the current session. To log yourself out, use the normal exit command instead. Use show session to display the list of current sessions and obtain valid session-ids. Access mode is Operational mode. Example: kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212.

Use the message command in Operational mode: message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]. By default the message is broadcast to all CLI sessions (target default is all), so message "System will reboot in 5 minutes" reaches everyone logged in over CLI. message-content is a string of 1-4096 characters. target accepts: all (all CLI sessions), local (only local sessions, serial console or CRAFT), remote (only remote sessions, e.g. SSH), a session-id (only that specific session), or a username (all CLI sessions of that user). The command can also be executed from NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only sent to CLI sessions. Targeted example: message "System reboot in 5 minutes" 0.0.0.0:36.

property entities are type-specific properties auto instantiated by the system but configurable by the user. Syntax: show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description] and set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]; access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Two property-names are supported. fast-client-recovery indicates if fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures; values are disabled or enabled, default disabled. max-packet-length indicates the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO; range 1518 to 18000, default 1518. Example: set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled.

Use run, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Pre-condition: the task or the script to be called must be defined. Syntax: run task [[task-name=]<value>] and run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]. task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name; script-name is a relative path to the script directory, with optional arguments. Flags: -q runs the CLI script in quiet mode (only command output shown, otherwise both the command and its output are shown); -r is a replace operation, executing the script as a declarative config script that replaces system configuration with the script content; -e sets the error option, continue (default), stop, or rollback. Examples: run task collect-diag; run script config.cli -e=stop -q.

Both add/set/show/delete user-configurable scheduled commands, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and share enabled (true/false, default true), command, command-type (CLI), frequency in w/d/h/m/s, start-time, end-time, persistent (default true, task survives a system restart), plus the reported task-status, next-run, previous-run, previous-result and previous-output. task is the individual scheduled-task entity: add task-<name> command <value> [label] [alarm-report-control] [frequency] [number-of-runs] ..., and it adds label, alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed) and number-of-runs (no-limit or 1..65535, default no-limit); its task-status is scheduled/disabled/finished/ongoing (default scheduled) and previous-result is success or fail. scheduled-task is the container form, add/set/delete scheduled-task-<name> with show scheduled-tasks; there task-status is true/false (default false), previous-result is 1 or 2, and an empty frequency (the default) means a single-occurrence task.

Only if you are an SA user. show session lists the currently established management layer sessions, but only SA users can access the list of all sessions; remaining users can only see their own session. Syntax: show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]; access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. session-id is the IP address and transport layer port of the session, or 'NA' if the session was initiated from the serial port. session-type can be cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui or gnmi; session-protocol can be telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https or http. RESTCONF sessions are visible in CLI if Cookie Based Authentication is used; that session has a 5 minute keep-alive by default, changeable with the restconf cookie-timeout attribute.

Yes. set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...] can set an attribute on multiple instances simultaneously using wildcards (*): as replacement of the whole instance key (card-*), as replacement of a single instance key (port-1-4-*, port-1-*-3), as replacement of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), for auto-completing instance keys (user-admin*, ethernet-*), and for auto-completing attribute names (admin* instead of admin-state). You can also use [] for ranges (card-1-[1..4]) or lists (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]). Filters of the form <attribute>=<value> restrict the change to matching entities, e.g. set port port-type=line admin-state lock, or set port-1-4* admin-state lock. All attribute-value pairs must belong to the same managed entity; with no entity id the currently scoped entity is used. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances; -f forces without confirmation and -v only validates.

User access to the shell command can be limited to users in the NA, NE, and TT user-groups. shell [-h] [shell command] runs in Operational mode and launches a Linux bash shell from within the CLI, using the currently logged in user and allowing the commands accessible to that user; closing it the typical way (exit) returns to the CLI prompt. A single shell command can also be executed inline, e.g. shell ifconfig, shell vi, shell editor. Certain commands/scripts can be launched with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo', limited to /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient, and the /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts (download.sh, install_os.sh, config_ip.sh, config_dns.sh, docker.sh, CopyLogsToUSB.sh and others). Use single quotes for composed commands: shell 'sudo netstat -alnp | grep sshd'.

Yes. If a user executes a show command which generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Narrow the request rather than retrying: address an individual <entity-id> instead of a generic <entity-type>, add one or more filters (<attribute>=<value>), bound recursion with -r=<n> (n levels down; full recursion if n is omitted), or reduce what is printed with -c (container instances only), -a (attributes only), -x (configuration/read-write attributes only) or -o (state/read-only attributes only). Since R9.0 show output is sorted numerically; a single managed entity is displayed in list format and multiple entities in tabular format. For readability, pipe long output, for example show -r | more.

Yes, with simulate, in Operational mode. Syntax: simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>]). trigger values are raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru and plug-out-fru, but note that plug-out-fru is not supported. For equipment simulation you provide the holder-AID (string 1..64) matching the card slot or the tom port, and the card type; subtype is optional (real hardware always has the subtype well defined). For alarms you provide alarmed-entity and alarm-type; if either is omitted when clearing alarms, all simulated alarms are cleared. alarm-direction and alarm-location default to auto, selected automatically by the system. The command works both in a simulator and on a real system, but on a real system the simulation cannot be done if it interferes with real HW, for example you cannot simulate plugout of hardware physically present. Example: simulate plug-in-fru 1-5.

Yes. sleep <time in seconds> specifies a delay for the given amount of time, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number. sleep 0.1 gives a 100 millisecond delay; sleep 1 gives one second. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, so it can be used in scripts in either mode. sleep -h displays help for the command. The guide states no minimum or maximum for the delay value beyond it being an arbitrary floating point number of seconds.

Add a task with a start-time and no frequency: frequency is what makes a task periodic, so leaving it unset gives a single-occurrence task. The guide's example is exactly this case: add task-db_backup_once command "upload database file-server=xfr1" start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label "DB Backup once". The command requires that the file server xfr1 be configured beforehand. Field limits: name is a string of 0..64 characters, command 1..1024 characters, command-type is cli, enabled defaults to true, persistent defaults to true so the task survives a system restart, alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited (default allowed). number-of-runs only applies when frequency is configured. Afterwards, show task-db_backup_once reports task-status (it becomes finished for an executed single-occurrence task), next-run (never), previous-run, previous-result (success or fail) and previous-output.

terminate (Operational mode) stops these running operations: terminate location-led <entity> ends a location led test previously started with the activate command on a chassis or a particular card, and has no effect if no test is active; terminate otdr [entity=]<value> stops an ongoing OTDR measurement on the given port; terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value> stops a manually triggered OTDR based Raman fiber check on an OTS-R entity, aborting the scan abruptly, restoring the otdr ne function attributes, reverting ots-r-auto-otdr auto-otdr-state to its previous state (re-raising PUMPS-DISABLED-OTDR-TEST-FAILED if that state was fail), while logs and available OTDR result files are saved; terminate loopback [entity=]<value>[,<value>]* terminates WSS loopback on NMC entities, and all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated; terminate cable-id stops a CableID verification test. Confirm the CableID stop with show cable-id cable-id-status: the test is known to be terminated once cable-id-state changes to idle. Verification runs per port-pair, so the current port-pair test finishes first and the maximum delay to terminate is one port-pair verification time. Examples: terminate location-led card-1-1; terminate otdr 1-1.3-7.

update applies a specific predefined attribute action chosen by <type>, rather than assigning an arbitrary value to a named attribute the way set does, and it runs in Operational mode only (set is also available in Candidate Configuration mode). Syntax: update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*], and multiple instances can be selected with a wildcard (*). The supported type values are: span-loss-alarm-threshold, which updates (re-evaluates) the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold; filter-insertion-date-now, which updates the chassis's dust filter insertion date to the current date; set-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to the under commissioning state, applicable to NEs entities in SLTE systems; and clear-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to the Ready for Service state, also for SLTE NEs entities. Examples: update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line; update filter-insertion-date-now chassis.

Use the auxiliary commands tic and toc, both available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. tic starts a timer for the typed command; toc displays the elapsed time since the timer was started and the command was executed by the system. Put them around the command on one line, separated by semicolons: tic;show log;toc. The same pattern times a list of commands or a script as a whole, for example tic ;show log ;traceroute 10.128.1.1 ;toc.

Yes. help -s <keyword> [<keyword> ...] searches the provided keyword(s) in all commands help text and displays the matches, in order of relevance. Partial keywords can be provided using a wild card, for example help -s inventory or help -s data*. The rest of the help system: ? on its own displays the list of all available commands; help <command/container/attribute> explains how it can be used (help show); <command> ? displays the possible addressable parameters (show ?); <command> -? displays the possible options (show -?); <command> -h displays the complete help (show -h); <command> <container> ? displays the hierarchy sub-containers and attribute list of the container; <command> <attribute> ? displays the list of attributes of the given container.

Yes to both: aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so your short name survives logout and other operators see it too. The alias command (Operational mode) defines a more user-friendly alphanumeric string for one or more commands, a container, an attribute, or values. Syntax: alias [-h] or alias [<name>=<value>]. alias with no arguments prints the current list of aliases in the form 'name=value'. Multi word values must be quoted: alias s=show, alias sa='show alarm'. Aliases can reference other aliases, and the <name> of an alias can be used without resolving it by putting it in quotes. Remove aliases with the unalias command.

unalias -a removes all defined aliases. The syntax is unalias -h, unalias -a, or unalias [<name> ...], so you can also remove one by name (unalias foo) or several at once (unalias bar baz qux). Access mode is Operational Mode. Removing an alias has impact on all sessions and users: aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so unalias -a clears the alias list for everyone on the node, not just your own session. The command is always successful unless a supplied <name> is not a defined alias. Aliases are added and visualized with the alias command.

Use tree [-a|-o|-d=depth] ([<entity id> ...]). -d=depth sets the maximum display depth of the tree, specifying the number of levels to be displayed; if not specified all levels are displayed by default. For example tree -d=2 shows two levels from the currently scoped entity. -a displays entity ancestors only, that is only the target entity along with all its ancestors, e.g. tree -a interface-DCN or tree -a port usb. -o displays a tree based on a YANG top node. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The base of the tree is the current working entity or the provided entity id (tree card-1-1); only managed entities are shown, including all existing instances, with no attribute names or values, and output uses the UTF-8 character set. You can also page it with tree | more.

edit <entity-id> [<entity-id> ...] navigates to any entity in the managed entity hierarchy. The ids can be absolute, starting from the root of the system (edit card-1-1, edit port-1-5-T1), or relative to the current entity shown in the path banner (edit chassis-1 slot-2); an attempt to edit a nonexistent entity instance will fail. up brings the current path up by one path level, to the parent of the currently selected entity; it supports no parameters and has no impact at the hierarchy top level. top brings the current path straight to the top of the managed entity hierarchy, [ne]. All three run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and the effect of each is visible on the CLI path banner: edit card-1-5 gives [ card-1-5 ], up gives [ equipment ], a further up or a top gives [ ne ].

Run history to display the current session's command history as a numbered list, then repeat an entry with '!<n>', where n is the number in the history list. '!!' repeats the previous command. history takes no parameters other than -h and runs in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. To find a particular entry in a long list, filter with piped commands, for example history | include 'show'.

Nothing happens: at the hierarchy top level the up command has no impact, and the path stays at [ne]. up brings the current path up by one path level, changing the currently selected managed entity to its parent, and its effect is visible on the CLI banner. So from [ card-1-5 ], up gives [ equipment ], the next up gives [ ne ], and any further up leaves you there. The command supports no parameters other than -h and runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands: edit navigates to any entity in the hierarchy, and top brings you straight to the hierarchy root [ne].

The filtering itself is identical: both are piped commands (<command> | grep <filter> and <command> | include <filter>) that only display lines matching <filter>, and the guide states each is the same as the other. In both, the filter may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed in quotes, the filter supports regex, multiple piped commands can be used in a single command, and the comparison is case insensitive, so show | grep abc and show | grep ABC are equivalent. The difference is that grep has several additional filtering options: -a=<n> the number of lines of context to show after the actual match, -b=<n> the number of lines of context to show before the actual match, and -n to display line numbers in the result. include accepts only the filter (plus -h). Related piped commands: exclude, begin and until.

Yes. Pipe the output through the `display` piped command using the `commands` mode: `<command> | display <mode>`. The `commands` mode displays the configurations as CLI 'set' and 'add' commands, and is specifically useful for creating CLI scripts from the current configuration. The documented example for producing a CLI script from all system configurations is `show -r | display commands`. Other supported modes on the same pipe are list (the default, one value per line), table, csv, keys-table, single-table, only-values, xml, json, xpath and interactive. `<command> | display -h` shows help for the pipe.

Yes. Combine the `begin` and `until` piped commands, which are explicitly documented as usable together to retrieve a sub-set of an output. `<command> | begin <words>` displays the output of the previous command starting from a specified word, and the output begins with the line that matches the word. `<command> | until <words>` displays the output ending at a specified word, and the output ends with the line that matches the word. For both, `<words>` is the line to begin with or end with, and may contain spaces if in quotes. Each also accepts `-h` to display help. Examples: `show | begin ne-location` and `show | until ne-location`.

Yes, and position matters. Use `<command> | more [-h]` to display long outputs incrementally, page by page. Multiple piped commands can be used sequentially, but `more` needs to be the last one in the command line, as in `tree | include led | more`. The page size matches exactly the size of the CLI session window, i.e., it is related to the terminal size, except for the serial port case where the terminal size is fixed. When the page limit is reached the display pauses; press any key to resume, or [CTRL]+[C] to terminate the display and return to the prompt. <enter> shows the next line, while any other key (including <space>, <tab>) shows the next page. `-h` displays help.

It does not fail: with the `sort` piped command, if an unrecognized attribute name is used it will be ignored. Syntax is `<show command> | sort [-h]` or `<show command> | sort [-i] [<attribute>*]`, where `<attribute>` is any attribute name that exists in the context of the output. To flip the order use `-i`, which inverts the order in the output and can be used on its own or together with an attribute list. `sort` without parameters displays the output sorted by object instance, the same as the default display. Examples: `show port | sort port-type`, `show user | sort -i user-group last-login-date`, and `show odu | sort -i`.

Capitalisation does not matter and patterns are supported. The `exclude` piped command (`<command> | exclude <filter>`) filters out lines containing the given word or string. `<filter>` does a case insensitive comparison, so `show | exclude abc` and `show | exclude ABC` are equivalent. The filter supports regex (regular expressions), and may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed by quotes, e.g. `show | exclude 'ne oper'`. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. `-h` displays help. The inverse commands are `include` and `grep`, which filter the output that includes the filtering text and behave the same way regarding case and regex.

Use the `highlight` piped command, which visually marks up a word or set of words in the output of the previous command: `<command> | highlight <word> [<word>]`. More than one word can be provided. Without quotes the words are searched for separately, so `show odu | highlight odu4 oduflex` highlights 'odu4' and 'oduflex' individually. To mark up a whole phrase, enclose it in quotes so it is searched for as a sentence: `<word>` may contain spaces if enclosed by quotes. The two forms can be mixed, as in `show odu | highlight 'idle lower-layer-down' odu4`, which highlights the sequence of words 'idle lower-layer-down' plus the word 'odu4'. `<command> | highlight -h` displays help.

Yes. The `linenum` piped command adds line numbers to the output of the previous command. Syntax is `<command> | linenum`, where `<command>` is any display command such as tree or show; `<command> | linenum -h` displays help for the command. The documented example of displaying an output with enumerated lines is `show | linenum`. Alternatively, if you are already filtering with `grep`, that command has a `-n` option which displays line numbers in the result, alongside `-a=<n>` and `-b=<n>` for lines of context after and before the actual match.
